items.text:
Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
- Published
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."
In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".
It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".
Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.
Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.
Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.
Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.
"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.
He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.
The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.
Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

items.text:
Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school
November 28, 2026
An explosion near a middle school on Saturday in Afghanistan's eastern Kunar province killed at least seven students and injured nearly 100 others, according to the Interior Ministry.
Early reports cited by the ministry's spokesperson indicate the blast was caused by negligent storage of explosives at a depot near the school belonging to a mining company in the Andir Sir area of the provincial capital, Asadabad.
No further details were provided on what caused the explosives to ignite.
Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at around 10 a.m.
Unverified video footage posted on social media showed injured children being taken to the provincial hospital.
Samiulhaq Haqbayan, provincial director for information, told Germany's DPA news agency that the explosives were intended for use in mining operations and for clearing hazardous rocks from mountain slopes along the nearby Kunar-Nuristan highway.
Third blast near a school this week
The ministry said an investigation into the incident is ongoing and further details will be announced once it is completed.
Saturday's incident is the third explosion near educational facilities in Afghanistan in the past week.
Two separate blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah provinces killed a total of five students, with local officials attributing both incidents to unexploded ordinances left behind from previous conflicts.

Seven students killed and nearly 100 injured in explosion in Afghanistan, official says
ByJacob Phillips
- Published
At least seven students have been killed and 99 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, an official has said.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, a spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.
An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.

items.text:
New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.
Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.
The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.
And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.
"Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.
Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.
"There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.
In an interview with NPR, Piper contended that Republican attorneys generals' policies are still broadly supported by voters, but were overshadowed by the unpopularity of the rest of the GOP. He noted that Republican attorneys general candidates ran ahead of GOP candidates for governor and U.S. Senate in some states.
Following the midterm results, Republican attorneys general convened for their fall meeting in Dallas, Texas, where the outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, lost his bid for Senate. He will soon be replaced by a Democrat, Nathan Johnson.
Piper said attendees grimly reflected on their challenges while also strategizing how to position Republican attorneys general to support the GOP as 2028 approaches. He added that the Republican Attorneys General Association are watching for potential "lawfare" by Democrats, including changing the number of Supreme Court justices or welcoming new states into the Union.
"We have to have better quality of candidates at the top of the ticket," Piper said. "We have to have better message discipline, and we need other committees in Washington to focus on what RAGA has done, and that is making sure we're good stewards of resources."
Democratic attorneys general held their own conference in Chicago, which some attendees said was both a celebration of the Democratic victories and an orientation for the incoming Democratic attorneys general.
"While a lot of the focus turns to what's next in Washington, we understand and we're not naive to the fact that we will continue to have a critical role in protecting our republic," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul during a Nov. 19 press briefing with other Democratic attorneys general.
Johnson, the incoming Texas attorney general, said at the same briefing that the wins for Democrats in the state house and governor's mansion could prompt Republicans to cooperate on a "cleansing" anti-corruption agenda. But he also signaled he'd support legislation and legal challenges to President Donald Trump's efforts to build a wall in Big Bend National Park on Texas' border with Mexico.
The Texas attorney general has traditionally brought cases on behalf conservative legal causes that had wide-ranging impacts across the country. The office also served as a training ground for Republican legal talent. U.S. Sen. John Cornyn and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott both served as attorney general before seeking higher office, while Sen. Ted Cruz served as solicitor general in the office before running for Congress. Other staffers have gone on to serve as judges, law clerks and prosecutors.
"Texas was a major intellectual force for the Republican attorneys general, and that's not going to be easily replaced," said James Tierney, a professor at Harvard Law School who has advised more than thirty attorneys general from both parties on staffing and legal philosophy.
"There are a lot of very smart, good lawyers in various AG offices who are very conservative," said Tierney. "But they don't have the heft and the size and the number of attorneys that Texas brings, and so for them, it's a very significant loss."
For Democrats, the recent wins could transform how the states enforce laws, bring legal cases, and support or hinder the Trump administration.
"These new attorneys general are not going to be particularly favorable towards the Trump administration, and will take an oppositional position in a number of different cases," said Anthony Michael Kreis, a constitutional law professor at Georgia State University. That may mean direct lawsuits against the administration in coalition with other attorneys general, Kreis said.
Many incoming Democratic attorneys general campaigned on bringing cases against alleged price gouging and digital surveillance by companies, as well as a tougher approach to antitrust concerns. But they will also face pressure to listen to their local business communities–including major multinational corporations.

items.text:
World Club Challenge: Wakefield to take on Sydney Roosters at Headingley on February 19 in England vs Australia clash
Wakefield Trinity to make World Club Challenge debut after winning Super League Grand Final just three years after relegation to the Championship; opponents Sydney Roosters boast a record five wins in this match, level with Wigan Warriors; English clubs victorious in last three games
Saturday 28 November 2026 09:55, UK
Super League champions Wakefield Trinity will face Sydney Roosters in the World Club Challenge at Headingley on February 19.
A maiden appearance in the match between the winners of Super League and the NRL is Wakefield's reward for an astonishing season, which culminated in their 23-10 Grand Final victory over Warrington Wolves at Old Trafford in October, just three years after relegation to the Championship.
Trinity will be looking to make it four straight wins for English clubs in this contest.
- London Broncos confirmed as 15th Super League team
- Super League reveals start date and new play-off format
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream contract-free on NOW
St Helens pipped Penrith in 2023 before Wigan and Hull KR recorded wins over Penrith and Brisbane Broncos respectively in 2024 and 2026.
Wakefield owner Matt Ellis said: "The World Club Challenge is the most prestigious game in club rugby league and to be playing the most successful side in the fixture's history is an honour.
"This is the biggest night in Wakefield Trinity's history and it would be fantastic to see our supporters pack out Headingley and make the atmosphere spectacular."
Roosters CEO: This match holds special place in our history
Sydney Roosters boast a joint-record five World Club Challenge titles, matching Wigan's tally, and have never lost the match.
Roosters went back-to-back in 2019 and 2020, beating Wigan for the first of those triumphs and St Helens for the second.
Those successes came amid a run of seven wins in eight years for Australian sides, prior to Covid-19 postponing fixtures and then this current English monopoly.
Sydney Roosters CEO Joe Kelly, whose team won the inaugural edition in 1976, said: "The World Club Challenge holds a special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters, and we are incredibly proud of our record in this prestigious fixture.
"To return to England as reigning NRL Premiers with the opportunity to become six-time World Club champions is an exciting prospect for our entire club."
Wakefield said venues such as Leeds United's Elland Road and Barnsley's Oakwell were also considered to stage the game.
Headingley will host the match for a fourth time, with Leeds Rhinos having taken on Manly, Melbourne and North Queensland in previous editions.

items.text:
Gaza’s chess players survive a genocide and rebuild a community
Gaza’s chess players are returning to the sport after three years of genocide.
Gaza City – Raghad Rabie, 18, never expected to beat her chess coach, Raghad Adas, at chess. During the friendly match, Rabie deliberately left some of her pieces exposed to distract her opponent as she planned a move that would deliver a checkmate in two turns.
Her strategy worked, giving her confidence in her abilities as a chess player. But the match also reflected something bigger: The return of chess to Gaza after the Israeli genocide devastated sporting activities across the enclave.
Rabie began learning chess in August 2025, when she was displaced in southern Gaza. Looking for something new to learn and a way to occupy her time, she taught herself the basic rules online before joining a training course run by Adas.
“I had admired chess players for a long time and wanted to learn the game. I started on my own, then the course helped me improve,” she says.
She has since participated in two tournaments and dreams of becoming a chess grandmaster, the goal of every serious chess player, and representing Palestine internationally.
But pursuing that ambition in Gaza, still under an Israeli siege and subject to daily air attacks despite an October 2025 “ceasefire”, is difficult.
There is no permanent training venue for chess players, so weekly gatherings take place in different locations, including the Lord Cafe in the al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City.
To become an International Chess Federation (FIDE)-rated grandmaster, as Rabie hopes, requires thousands of hours of dedicated practice and study. But a shortage of chessboards, clocks and chess books – and soaring prices for any available chess equipment – has made this mission difficult.
Before the war, Adas was captain of the girls’ Spark team, playing in Palestinian Chess Federation tournaments. She was also among 10 players selected to take part in matches against other Palestinians from the occupied West Bank with the goal of forming a national team, which it was hoped would compete internationally.
Travel arrangements and permit procedures had been completed, but then Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza broke out in October 2023, killing at least 74,000 Palestinians and laying waste to the Palestinian enclave.
“I was excited about taking part in an international tournament, but the war made everything much more difficult,” Adas told Al Jazeera.
Adas said the team’s headquarters was destroyed, its players were scattered across Gaza, and she lost contact with several former teammates amid the forced Israeli displacements.
About a year after the war began, Adas started teaching chess in shelters, initially volunteering before working with organisations and eventually continuing her mission independently. She noticed a growing interest in the sport among newcomers, as well as the return of players who had stopped playing during the genocide.
This led her to establish “Stalemate” in February, a community chess initiative that began with 12 players and now boasts 470 members in its messaging group. Not all are active players; some are still learning or following its activities, but weekly get-togethers typically still attract between 20 and 40 participants.
These include children, young people, women and older players. Adas said she has noticed that the events have given people traumatised by the genocide a reason to leave their homes and meet other people again.
“I wanted chess to become a space that brings people together, rather than remaining a game limited to professionals or people who frequent cafes,” she said.
Stalemate has organised several competitive events, including an individual tournament on November 19 in Gaza City, which attracted 41 players. The competition consisted of nine rounds using the Swiss system to allow players to compete against players of a similar level.
The return of chess
Sharif Daher, deputy head of the Palestinian Chess Federation, said Gaza had more than 500 chess players before the war, including at least 200 regular players and about 20 clubs participating in local competitions.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has severely affected players and the venues where they used to meet and compete.
Nelly al-Masri, a federation member and spokesperson, said the destruction of sport facilities has made restarting activities extremely difficult, and the problems faced by Palestinians in Gaza run much deeper than returning to play the sport.
“The sport infrastructure in Gaza has been destroyed. The situation has become catastrophic and requires humanitarian relief work, not sports activities,” she told Al Jazeera.
Nevertheless, at the request of players, the federation has resumed training sessions and tournaments, despite limited funding, equipment and difficulties travelling between northern and southern Gaza, with Israel still strictly controlling movement.
The federation’s first official competition in Gaza since the war began was the aptly named “Return and Loyalty Tournament” in January 2026, which attracted more than 50 players. In June, the federation organised the Gaza Open Rapid Chess Championship, with 84 participants, followed in July by the eighth Musa Issa Saba Memorial Rapid Chess Championship, which attracted 92 players.
These tournaments helped bring former players back to the sport while introducing new faces to chess. However, the federation also lost players during the war, including member Walid Abu al-Hassan, a local chess champion who was killed along with his wife and two children in an Israeli air raid on their tent in Khan Younis in 2024.
Among those who have continued playing is 24-year-old Anas al-Rifi, who began learning chess in 2023 after a friend introduced him to the movement of the pieces on the board.
He developed his skills through YouTube tutorials, playing against more experienced opponents and learning from his mistakes.

items.text:
Yemen government forces hit Houthi positions as UN warns of hunger crisis
About 1.8 million people face emergency levels of hunger in government-held areas, according to the UN.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have launched multiple air strikes across Houthi-held territory, with at least 121 Houthis killed or injured over the past day.
Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said on Saturday that more than six Yemeni governorates were hit overnight by the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the government forces.
“In the capital, Sanaa, 13 people were injured, including three critically, who were rushed to a hospital after a gas station was hit in the Tahrir district. The attack also hit homes and shops,” he said.
The second air attack in Sanaa, according to the Houthis, killed a man and his wife after it hit their home, he added.
He also listed an attack on a fuel station in the district of Bani Matar, on the outskirts of Sanaa, a raid on the southern city of Taiz and five air raids in the strategic city of Mocha, along the Red Sea coastline, which targeted a power station.
The “Dawn of Yemen” government offensive comes as fighting has escalated in Yemen in the past months, with Saudi-led coalition forces ramping up operations against the Houthis.
At least 121 Houthis killed or injured
Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said earlier on Friday that government forces carried out 726 attacks against Houthi positions in the 24 hours prior, and claimed 121 fighters and commanders were killed or wounded. He added that fighting was ongoing in Ma’rib, al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahij, Shabwah, Midi and al-Dhale areas.
Houthi-affiliated media reported that a Saudi air strike killed 11 civilians, most of them children, in al-Turbah in Taiz governorate.
Al Jazeera could not confirm the death toll, and coalition forces did not comment.
Meanwhile, the government-run Saba news agency reported that Houthi attacks on government locations in Taiz on Saturday also resulted in the death of three civilians, including a 10-year-old boy. Three others, including an infant, were wounded.
Coalition officials added that a Houthi missile launched at Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh was intercepted and that Houthi attacks on government positions along the al-Masrakh district front, south of Taiz, were repelled.
The claims and casualties could not be independently verified.
Yemen sinks deeper into hunger crisis
Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July amid tensions surrounding the US-Israel war on Iran, and after a 2022 ceasefire collapsed.
The renewed violence has worsened an ongoing humanitarian crisis, with thousands displaced and the prices of food, fuel and other necessities soaring.
Aid groups warn the crisis has been deepened by dramatic aid cuts by donors like the United States and other Western countries in the past year.
The World Food Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization warned on Friday that Yemen is among nations facing the gravest risk of food insecurity, and that hunger is likely to worsen there over the next six months.
About 1.8 million people faced emergency levels of hunger in government-held areas, according to the agencies’ analysis. More than 300,000 people have been newly displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahij and Aden provinces, the report said.
The encirclement of the city of Taiz has created conditions resembling a siege, it warned, adding that Houthi-held areas were becoming harder to access and monitor, and that the group was holding 73 UN staff.
The Houthis encircled Taiz city in early October.
A UN assessment earlier in February had found 18.3 million people across the country – more than half the population – were in crisis or worse.

items.text:
Andy Hunter heard what Andoni Iraola and David Moyes had to say ahead of the Merseyside derby, the Spaniard’s first. Life in the city might have come unusually naturally for him, though: “In some ways,” Moyes said, “the Basques are like Scousers.”
“I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape.
“It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.”
It’s a particularly intriguing day in the Championship, where West Ham, bottom of the last-six-games form table with just two points in that time, play Stoke, who with five wins in five and a draw in the one before that are joint top. Similarly Lincoln, with three points in their last six one of three teams hovering just above the Hammers in that form table, play Wolves, who with 16 points are also joint top, in one of three lunchtime kick-offs. Meanwhile the two other teams with three points from their last six, Burnley and Millwall, play each other, while just above them on form Derby (24th and bottom of the actual table, 20th on form with four) host Watford (20th in the actual table, 18th on form also with four), who will be led for the first time by Edward Iordanescu and are seeking to improve on a hideous away record so far this season: one draw and seven defeats in eight.
Here’s our report on last night’s Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea. Chelsea conceded two penalties in the whole of last season, nobody conceded fewer; the one that led to Forest’s second goal last was already the third of this campaign, and nobody has conceded more.
Hello world! Another weekend dawns, and a Saturday with only three Premier League games, and none of the top five in action, but with plenty elsewhere to keep us occupied. We’ll also be looking back at Nottingham Forest’s victory over Chelsea last night, and ahead towards the six Premier League games scheduled for tomorrow, games that include the Merseyside derby, Manchester City heading to Arsenal, and … um … Crystal Palace v Hull!

The Art of Negotiation
What can we learn from successful peace deals? | Episode 2
Top conflict negotiators who brokered historic peace deals reveal the secrets to ending intractable wars.
Having worked on peace deals in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo and her homeland Northern Ireland, Kate Fearon knows firsthand that negotiations are never simple.
Now leading conflict prevention at OSCE, the world’s largest regional security group, the veteran mediator reflects on these gruelling processes.
“You need to take risks for peace. We’re all human and there’s always common ground. It can be very hard to see at the beginning. That’s where a mediator comes in,” Fearon says.
From Colombia to Mozambique, this Al Jazeera series meets the mediators who have prevailed against all odds to end wars, offering rare insights into what happens behind closed doors.

items.text:
Sudanese launch clean-up drive as rubbish overwhelms Khartoum’s streets
In litter-strewn Khartoum, disease and rubble threaten health.
Khartoum, Sudan – When Musa Abdelrahman, 54, returned to Khartoum in March via a government-organised repatriation scheme, he hoped the relative stability of the capital would mean his life could be rebuilt at home.
Abdelrahman lived close to Khartoum International Airport. When war broke out between former allies, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, his neighbourhood became one of the epicentres of the war in Sudan, which has now killed tens of thousands.
When Abdelrahman returned home from Egypt, he found a city with infrastructure and basic services ruined and exhausted. The most visible illustration of this was rubbish piling up on streets across the capital.
When rubbish collection trucks fail to arrive – which they inevitably do – neighbourhoods turn into open dumps with residents forced to endure foul smells and swarms of insects.
“The problem is not just about how the city looks; it has started affecting our daily lives,” Abdelrahman told Al Jazeera. “We want to live in a clean environment, with waste collection trucks operating regularly, rather than waiting for rubbish to pile up until it becomes a bigger problem.”
Breakdown in civil life
The war in Sudan has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with about nine million people currently displaced and poverty rates dropping to levels last seen in the 1980s.
Politically, the country remains divided between rival RSF and SAF administrations, but with resources focused on the war, civilian life has been decimated.
After the SAF recaptured the capital in March 2025 – and subsequently lifted a curfew and the state of emergency – residents perceived the city as safe enough to return to.
About 2.88 million people had returned to Khartoum State by October 28, 2026, the highest number among Sudan’s states. Khartoum and its neighbouring Omdurman have also been a refuge for millions of people fleeing the fighting currently embroiling western and southern Sudan.
Despite the relative stability in the capital now, widespread challenges remain in restoring basic services due to the destruction of infrastructure and the limited capacity of public services to meet growing needs, as thousands descend on Khartoum.
Refuse collection worker Saeed Koko said that public services are struggling to deal with the garbage crisis given their limited resources.
“Before the war, waste collection services covered most residential neighbourhoods in Khartoum, and rubbish was collected more regularly, although waste management had been a longstanding problem in the city for years,” he said.
“Today, waste collection vehicles mainly operate in the major markets, while many residential neighbourhoods are left without regular waste collection services. As a result, rubbish accumulates in streets and open spaces for long periods.”
The war has strained all public services in Khartoum, and Koko said refuse collectors lack the specialised workforce and equipment they had before the conflict.
“We need more waste collection vehicles, equipment and workers. The war displaced many workers, and we lost some of them because of the conflict,” he said.
Sawsan Omar, a woman who has returned to Omdurman, said residents in Khartoum State have resorted to burning piles of rubbish.
“Sometimes we cannot open the windows or sit outside because of the smells and smoke. What worries us most is the impact on children and older people,” Omar told Al Jazeera.
“We do not want to live surrounded by rubbish, nor should we have to breathe in the smoke from burning it. We appeal to the authorities to provide waste collection trucks and containers in residential neighbourhoods and ensure that rubbish is collected regularly. All we want is to live in a clean and safe environment and to feel that returning to our homes means returning to normal life.”
Disease risk
Dr Al-Fatih Mahmoud, a public health specialist, said that repeated exposure to toxic fumes and pollutants posed long-term health risks to residents.
“Inhaling these emissions can cause irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, coughing and shortness of breath. It can also worsen asthma, bronchitis and other respiratory conditions. Children, older people, pregnant women and individuals with pre-existing respiratory conditions are particularly vulnerable to these health risks,” said Mahmoud.
“Therefore, the continued accumulation and burning of waste in residential neighbourhoods constitute a public health threat that requires urgent intervention. This should include regular waste collection and removal, safe waste disposal methods, preventing waste burning in residential areas, strengthening health and environmental monitoring, and raising public awareness about the dangers of these practices.”
The current build-up of rubbish “creates favourable conditions for the breeding of flies, mosquitoes and rodents, increasing the risk of disease transmission and the spread of infections among residents,” Mahmoud told Al Jazeera.
“The decomposition of waste and its exposure to environmental factors, coupled with the possibility of pollutants seeping into water and food sources, may increase the risk of gastrointestinal diseases, including diarrhoea, gastroenteritis, typhoid and cholera. It may also contribute to the spread of insect-borne diseases such as dengue fever and malaria, depending on environmental conditions and the prevalence of disease-carrying vectors.”
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), in a report on conditions facing returnees to Khartoum, cited the lack of solid waste management services as a growing concern among residents and returnees.
Waste collection and transportation vehicles, maintenance workshops and spare parts warehouses have been damaged in fighting, while large numbers of waste containers were lost.

items.text:
India: Tight security at disputed Deepathoont lamp-lighting ceremony
Published November 28, 2026last updated November 28, 2026
What you need to know
Here is our weekend coverage of India on Saturday, November 28:
- A contentious stone pillar has stoked a legal, political and religious controversy in India’s Tamil Nadu
- A Hindu ceremony will take place at the pillar today at the direction of the Supreme Court
- An earlier order by the top court for the ritual lamp lighting to take place at the pillar was not followed
Supreme Court orders lamp lighting at Deepathoon, four days after festival
On Friday, the Supreme Court criticised the Tamil Nadu government and Madurai district officials for "wilful" defiance of the November 20 order and directed the lamp to be lit at Deepathoon on Saturday.
The Supreme Court suspended the Subramaniya Swamy temple's Board of Trustees and appointed a committee of two retired Madras High Court judges as receivers of the trust, who will oversee Saturday's ceremony.
The court also tweaked its earlier order and instead of a small team approved by the temple trust, has now permitted every devotee to light the lamp at Deepathoon on Saturday.
It has tasked the paramilitary CRPF with ensuring security at both the temple and the shrine ahead of the ceremony.
Modi posts Tamil devotional chant amid Deepathoon row
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote a post on X on last night, invoking Lord Murugan, one of the gods associated with Karthigai Deepam.
Without making any mention of the row, the Hindu nationalist leader wrote the traditional Tamil devotional chant "Victory to Lord Murugan, who wields the spear!" thrice, in English, Tamil and Hindi.
Tamil Nadu: Lamp lighting at controversial Deepathoon site today amid security presence
Personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were deployed at the Thiruparankundram hillock near Tamil Nadu state's Madurai, a day after the Supreme Court ordered a Hindu ceremonial lamp lighting to take place at a controversial stone pillar on Saturday.
At the heart of the row, is the Deepathoon (stone pillar) situated atop Thiruparankundram, and about 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah, a shrine associated with Sufism — a mystical tradition within Islam.
What is Tamil Nadu's stone pillar controversy?
The Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy temple, also located on Thiruparankundram, traditionally conducts the annual Tamil Hindu Karthigai Deepam (festival of lights) ceremony at the Deepa Mandapam site near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple, situated on the lower part of the hill.
But Hindu groups had sought permission to light the ceremonial lamp at Deepathoon.
On November 20, India's top court permitted the lighting at Deepathoon as a one-time arrangement, allowing a restricted team to conduct the ceremony there.
However, the lamp was lit at the usual Deepa Mandapam when the festival came on November 24 as the temple trustees decided to stick to what they assert is established practice.
The Tamil Nadu government, helmed by Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, also maintains that the customary spot for the ritual is near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple and had filed a review petition in the Supreme Court challenging its November 20 order.
Tuesday's lamp lighting led to protests by Hindu groups and also workers of theHindu Nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused the Vijay government of refusing to comply with the Supreme Court's directive.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, ushering you into India's newscape this weekend.
First, we dive into the developments coming out of the southern state of Tamil Nadu where a stone pillar is at the centre of political, legal and religious controversy.
Meanwhile there are rumblings in the power corridor of New Delhi as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet and his main rival, Congress party, have held meetings respectively, to talk tactics ahead of a sudden, special sitting of the parliament called at the request of the ruling government.
And India's Men in Blue are facing New Zealand's Black Caps for a second day of a high-stakes test cricket match at Hagley Oval in Christchurch.
Stay tuned as we bring you more.

items.text:
Ranking the Premier League's ultimate free-kick specialists
- Published
Dip, swerve, curl, whip. Hours spent mastering the craft of a great free-kick ensure those that ripple the back of the net are particularly satisfying.
This week we are digging into the Premier League's all-time best takers.
The number of goals scored from direct free-kicks has gradually decreased over the past two decades (boo!) with a rising focus on generating higher-quality chances, rather than having a pop from range.
It is perhaps unsurprising then that James Maddison is the only current player in the competition's all-time top 25 free-kick scorers, after James Ward-Prowse returned to Championship side Southampton in the summer.
Dominik Szoboszlai, however, is bucking the trend with five since joining Liverpool from 32 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 15.6% and almost a third of his total Premier League goals.
He looks on course to become a free-kick great, already only one goal behind Trent Alexander-Arnold and Leighton Baines and just two off the likes of Matt le Tissier, Wayne Rooney and Steven Gerrard.
The majority of top scorers hail from the halcyon era of, essentially, having a dig.
Yaya Toure belongs in another category - he misses out on the top 10 below but could be deemed a 'one-season wonder' in this realm, despite having eight years at Manchester City.
His prolific spell in 2013-14 deserves recognition, scoring four of his seven free-kick attempts that term - a staggering 57.1% conversion rate and by far the Premier League's best since Opta began collecting such data in 2006.
There is also an honourable mention for Louis Saha, the only man in the Premier League era to score a free-kick with each foot - with his left for Manchester United against Southampton in January 2004, and with his right for Everton against Fulham seven years later.
And while we are here, these are the goalkeepers who least liked facing them.
What we are looking for, though, are the real free-kick specialists - those players whose names evoke memories of ball meeting top bins.
For that reason, despite sitting joint-third on the scorers list with 12, Cristiano Ronaldo and Thierry Henry do not make it. They just scored too many goals - and too many great ones - to be renowned specifically for their set-pieces.
Fewer than 7% of Henry's 175 Premier League goals were free-kicks, netting one on average every 21.5 games. Ronaldo, meanwhile, tried his luck 167 times, scoring one roughly every 14 attempts.
So let's get stuck into the top 10.
The first spot up for grabs could have gone several ways - Maddison, as mentioned, has a decent shout to be included, and likewise Christian Eriksen who netted eight in the Premier League and also laid on 13 free-kick assists.
Frank Lampard has nine goals but also the most attempts on record - and the data only accounts for half his Premier League career.
Instead, I've gone for...
10. Ashley Young
OK, the case for Ashley Young is in his longevity - he curled in a free-kick during the play-offs to help Watford win promotion in 2006 and was still scoring them almost two decades later.
At 39 years and 148 days old, Young became the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick in Everton's win over Wolves in December 2024. His seventh successful free-kick strike in the competition and the final effort of his 50-goal top-flight haul.
Young holds a decent conversion rate, scoring with 10.3% of his 68 top-flight attempts, while also chipping in with nine free-kick assists - only a handful of players have more since 2003-04.
Young's set-piece duties also tend to bookend his career. A trusted specialist at Watford and Aston Villa, he fell behind Ronaldo, Rooney and co at United but still popped up with a memorable long-range free-kick against the Hornets, his boyhood club.
9. Nolberto Solano
Nolberto Solano netted nine times from free-kicks in the Premier League - although that tally may have been higher had he not shared set-piece duties with Laurent Robert for a chunk of his Newcastle career, while Alan Shearer chipped in too.
In fact, including spells at Aston Villa and West Ham, the Peruvian scored 18% of his top-flight goals with free-kicks.
He had a decent conversion rate. Opta data only goes back to 2003-04, but since then Solano, who also played for Aston Villa and West Ham, netted 10% of all his free-kick attempts on goal.
8. Juan Mata
Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard reckons Juan Mata is the best free-kick taker in Premier League history and the only player who outshines current Anfield star Szoboszlai.
I disagree, hence ranking the Spaniard eighth, but Mata can claim to be the most ruthless - he's scored a higher percentage of free-kicks than any player to have had at least 20 attempts since the stat-counting began in 2003-04.
The World Cup winner, who recently retired, netted eight in the English top flight from 49 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 16.3%.
7. Morten Gamst Pedersen
Morten Gamst Pedersen was plucked from the freezing fjords above the Arctic Circle to score bangers for Blackburn, a left foot as crisp as the icy waters surrounding his former home in Tromso.
The hair-gelled Norwegian netted 34 Premier League goals in eight seasons at Ewood Park, with just shy of 30% of those coming from free-kicks - the fifth-highest proportion in the competition's history.
It puts the winger eighth on the all-time list with 10 goals from 158 free-kick shots - only Lampard and Ronaldo have attempted more since 03-04.
6. Gianfranco Zola
The diminutive Italian announced himself to the Premier League as he meant to go on. In his fourth Chelsea appearance, Gianfranco Zola scored his first goal from a belting long-range free-kick against Everton.
It was the first of 12 in the competition.
What sets Zola apart is all of those came after turning 30, having been a phenomenal set-piece specialist back in Serie A - he remains sixth on the all-time list there with 20, one behind Roberto

items.summary:
UN’s Albanese leaves Costa Rica airport after constitutional court verdict
Albanese leaves the Costa Rican airport where she has been held after the court orders her to be released from the premises.
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territ
items.text:
UN’s Albanese leaves Costa Rica airport after constitutional court verdict
Albanese leaves the Costa Rican airport where she has been held after the court orders her to be released from the premises.
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, has left Costa Rica’s Santamaria airport after being denied entry to the country and spending a second night held up there.
Costa Rica’s move on Thursday to hold Albanese at the airport put the small Central American country’s increasingly close alignment with the United States and Israel on security and foreign policy into the spotlight.
“I’m outside the airport. Finally. Thank you to everyone who helped me,” Albanese said on X at about 07:00 GMT on Saturday, after sending a series of posts from the airport serving the capital city, San Jose.
She wrote earlier, at about 04:00 GMT, that the Constitutional Court of the country ordered her to “be let out to go to a hotel and rest and the immigration police does not let me”, adding: “Am I detained? HELP?”
She also said Air France staff were “actively ignoring” the Constitutional Court ruling with excuses, adding that she had been awake for more than 50 hours.
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said on Friday he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport.
The UN Human Rights Office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on “claimed national security grounds”.
Albanese, in another post on X, lamented the uncomfortable conditions in the airport, adding that she was “counting the hours till my flight tomorrow”, without specifying the destination.
But the Constitutional Chamber of Costa Rica’s Supreme Court confirmed late on Friday that her destination would be Mexico when it issued a second interim order, directing that she be transferred to a hotel, according to the AFP news agency.
She had previously told local media that she intended to travel on to Mexico, but that immigration authorities told her she needed to return to France, to which she objected.
Albanese also said authorities took her passport and that she was offered a detention room to sleep.
The US-aligned government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an “international alert over links to terrorist acts”.
Italian embassy assisting Albanese
The Italian Embassy in Costa Rica is providing consular assistance to Albanese after Costa Rican authorities denied her entry, the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday.
The ministry said the Italian ambassador contacted Albanese and sent a consular official to the airport to help.
Italian officials have repeatedly urged Costa Rican authorities to allow her entry, but Albanese remains in the airport’s international transit area and has not formally entered the country, it added.
Albanese had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica.
A UN special rapporteur is an independent expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate and report on rights abuses in a specific country.
Albanese, who has been sanctioned by the US under measures related to the International Criminal Court, said she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision and rejected what she described as efforts to link her to “terrorism”.
Albanese has become one of the most outspoken international critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, making her a frequent target of pro-Israel officials and governments. Israel’s UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica’s decision in a post on X.

items.title: Basque to the future: Andoni Iraola fired up for first Merseyside derby
items.summary: “I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Li
items.text:
“I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape.
“It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.”
That has rarely been a problem of late for Liverpool, who have lost one of their past 15 visits to Everton and showed with last season’s 100th-minute winner from Virgil van Dijk that a move to a new stadium does not necessarily mean a fresh start.
Iraola has identified parallels with the Basque derby not only through this week’s encounters with an approving public. The Liverpool head coach says of Athletic v Sociedad: “It is a massive game for us and it’s a bit like here – you know a lot of people on the other side. I have a lot of friends who are Real Sociedad and they have a lot of friends who are Athletic. I think it’s quite a natural rivalry. The relationship between them is normally quite good but everyone wants to win that game.”
David Moyes, who managed Real Sociedad for 12 months from November 2014, offers a comparison that extends beyond football. “In some ways, the Basques are like scousers,” the Everton manager says. “They compete with each other and they are rivals but they see themselves as being different from the rest of the country. There is a bit of camaraderie between them. But it is a fierce derby and a huge game.
“The thing about Real Sociedad, nearly all your players have to be Basque. Bilbao are pure Basque but we had incredible players coming through ourselves. We gave a debut to [Mikel] Oyarzabal. They had an incredible setup. There are very few teams in the Premier League who could do what Sociedad do in terms of bringing kids through the ranks.”
Moyes had a habit of frustrating but not beating his local rivals during his time in the Basque country, which has echoes of his record in the Merseyside derby. That reads four wins, nine draws and 16 defeats across two spells with Everton. All three of his games in charge of Real Sociedad versus Athletic ended in draws, with the first two featuring a red card. Iraola played in the second, in April 2015, when La Real had a man sent off but fought back to draw 1-1 at San Mamés in the last of his 12 seasons with his boyhood club.
Despite being born only 10km from San Sebastián, and 100km from Bilbao, there was no question which Basque club Iraola was destined to represent. “It was always Athletic for me,” he says. “I went there very young and I never played for the academy of Real Sociedad. I have a lot of friends who went on to play for Real Sociedad but at my club, Antiguoko, in that moment and also now, it was like an Athletic Club team. The connections mean if you are good at Antiguoko you will go through the Athletic Club system. I was lucky enough to arrive there and spend 16 years in Bilbao.”
The Merseyside rivals enter the 249th edition of England’s most-played derby on the back of starkly contrasting weeks. Whereas Everton suffered the heaviest defeat of Moyes’s second spell as manager in Monday’s 4-0 hammering at Brentford, where they also produced arguably their worst performance since the Scot’s return, Liverpool have plundered seven goals without reply in commanding victories against Manchester United and Club Brugge. Their away form under Iraola also augurs well for a fourth successive win over Everton for the first time since a run to August 1991.
Liverpool have won their past four fixtures on the road and six from eight in all competitions, scoring 21 times. And it is not only their pace, Florian Wirtz’s growing influence and Alexander Isak’s predatory qualities in attack that have made the difference away from Anfield. No team have conceded fewer goals on their travels in the Premier League this season than Liverpool, with four. The additions of Jérémy Jacquet and Ronald Araújo have improved Liverpool’s resilience as well as their defending at set pieces, both of which will be important at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday.
“I don’t think there is a big difference in our performances away or at home,” Iraola says. “Normally you will find more spaces when you play away because teams are braver and they press you more. But sometimes they can press you and you will feel more uncomfortable. I prefer to play at home even if we have better numbers away at the moment. Also at home we have had difficult games in terms of having big games, but the way we play doesn’t really change a lot.
“Derbies are always different. It doesn’t matter where you are in the standings, it doesn’t matter the run that you are in. Normally, this type of game is different and you can feel it from the beginning. We have to be very competitive, we have to win our duels and be at a good level because everyone wants to win this game.”

items.title: The Renéessance is over but Arsenal’s chaotic cycle will go on without further change | Suzanne Wrack
items.summary: The Renéessance is over. Three down, how many more to go? The exit of Arsenal manager, Renée Slegers, 18 months after delivering European glory was somewhat inevitable, her position made untenable after six home draws in six games and just 15 points from 11 games, but will it solve the Gunners’ prob
items.text:
The Renéessance is over. Three down, how many more to go? The exit of Arsenal manager, Renée Slegers, 18 months after delivering European glory was somewhat inevitable, her position made untenable after six home draws in six games and just 15 points from 11 games, but will it solve the Gunners’ problems?
There were high expectations in north London prior to the season, after difficult starts in back-to-back WSL campaigns put them outside a real title challenge within the opening few games.
There was frustration at their early sluggishness in previous seasons, but there were also asterisks next to each campaign; injury crises stifling things, players going far in a major tournament leaving the club with a stunted pre-season and Champions League qualifying campaigns also cutting into that vital pre-season preparation and players’ time off.
This year, there were no excuses. Qualification for the Champions League league phase was secured with a second-place finish in the WSL. Other than Élisa de Almeida, who arrived from Paris Saint-Germain, their summer transfer business was done early. No major international tournament in the summer gave them a full pre-season with a close to full squad.
That transfer business was applauded, too, although there were eyebrows raised at the decision to let go of Beth Mead and Katie McCabe, two of their strongest performers last season, with a late attempt to reverse on the latter’s exit a complete mess The arrivals lifted spirits.
The recruitment of Georgia Stanway, Selina Cerci, Lisa Baum and Géraldine Reuteler from Bayern Munich, TSG Hoffenheim, RB Leipzig and Eintracht Frankfurt, respectively, and Ona Batlle from Barcelona, and goalkeepers Isabella Damm and Misa Rodríguez from Brøndby and Real Madrid, in addition to De Almeida, demonstrated their title-chasing ambition.
How, then, does a starting XI packed with so much talent and with a bench as stacked, fall so short? A squad with so much depth that the HB Køge manager, Kristian Mørch, said, after his side faced the 2025 Champions League winners on 22 September: “We laughed when we saw the lineup and started joking that it must be one of the strongest benches ever in the Women’s Champions League.”
After Joe Montemurro and Jonas Eidevall, Slegers is the next manager to be shown the door after a period of underperformance. The difference this time is the clamouring for managerial change was far quieter than her predecessors experienced because many believe Arsenal’s problems are far greater than the manager.
Slegers also delivered one of the greatest moments in the club’s history, leading them to Champions League glory with a stunning 1-0 defeat of reigning champions Barcelona in May 2025, having taken charge, initially on an interim basis, the preceding October.
It was the most exhilarating of moments for Arsenal fans, who had had to wait for the club that had set the standard for so many years to lift a major trophy again. That victory should have been a launchpad for further success, instead Arsenal have gone backwards, failing to overhaul the squad in the season which followed and then, arguably, failing in their attempt to overhaul it this summer.
Slegers is not blame free. The minimal minutes handed to players such as Reuteler and Cerci have been hugely frustrating after the fanfare with which they arrived and the lack of use of Reuteler in particular has felt almost cruel at times. In addition, tactical decisions haven’t made an impact and an inability to light a fire under the beleaguered players has been evident.
Ultimately though, the blame lies with those higher up. Under Montemurro, Eidevall and Slegers, all talented managers who began with so much promise, when things started to turn, there was talk of internal reviews, investment, a reset and work being done to find solutions. Except despite those reviews and any changes that were made as a result, here we are, on groundhog day. Those higher up need to take a healthy portion of responsibility for Slegers’ position eventually becoming untenable.
In letting Slegers go, Arsenal are losing a young manager with lots of developing still to do but also huge potential. They are also losing a manager who gets the club, a manager who spent time in the academy as a player and who wears a silver ring with the 1936-49 Arsenal crest on it on her little finger.
Her future is bright. What’s in Arsenal’s future without greater change is unclear. The former London City Lionesses and Brighton manager Melissa Clarke-Reed, who has been part of Arsenal’s coaching staff since 2004, has been named interim manager, with assistant Aaron D’Antino also leaving after eight years at the club.
Possible replacements include a vocally available Nick Cushing, who led Manchester City to a first league title in 2016, the former Manchester United manager Marc Skinner, and the former Bayern Munich and Angel City manager Alexander Straus. Though they may choose to wait and try to lure someone already in post elsewhere such as Casey Stoney (Canada), Laura Harvey (Seattle Reign) or Juan Carlos Amorós (Gotham FC). Whoever comes in, if great change doesn’t come with them, then it would be reasonable to expect that after any initial positivity Arsenal’s chaotic cycle will continue.

items.text:
At least six students killed in blast beside school in Afghanistan’s Kunar
Official says the figures were preliminary and the casualty numbers could change as more information becomes available.
At least six students have been killed and 97 others injured in an explosion next to a school in eastern Afghanistan’s Kunar province, according to a medical official speaking to Al Jazeera.
Mawla Dad, the head of Kunar Provincial Hospital, told Al Jazeera on Saturday that the figures were initial and the casualty numbers could change as more information becomes available.
The explosion occurred in a house beside a middle school in the Andar Ser area of Kunar province, eastern Afghanistan, at about 10am (05:30 GMT) on Saturday, Mawlawi Sami-ul-Haq, the director of Information and Culture in Kunar, told Al Jazeera separately.
He said the house belonged to people involved in mining operations who had stored dynamite there.
Sami-ul-Haq did not provide further details about the incident, including the number of casualties or the extent of the damage. He added that no further information was available at the time.
Investigative teams from Kunar province, which is located on the border with Pakistan, were at the scene.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital of Kabul wounded more than 40 children aged between nine and 14.

items.text:
Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
- Published
Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.
The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.
Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."
They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.
WWE has been contacted for further comment.
Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.
The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.
Owens said Haley loved performing.
"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.
"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."
WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"
WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."
WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.
Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X.
According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November.
He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl.
Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019.
He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.
Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September.
No cause of death was provided at the time.

items.text:
How dad's embarrassment was making of Gross at Brighton
- Published
Many people will have parents to thank for shaping them into who they are today, but for Pascal Gross it was his dad's embarrassment when watching him play that turned out to be the making of him at Brighton.
It was not that Gross senior was not proud of his son, but he was unhappy with how he acted on the pitch in one of his first games with the Seagulls after signing for them in the summer of 2017.
"He went to the game. He went to every game," Gross said in The Football Interview.
"It was Leicester away and I was on the floor constantly like a little child crying for free-kicks and did nothing.
"I think my dad must've spoken to a couple fans. He said he was my dad and stuff. But then on the way back [from the game], he said he covered himself with the programme. He said it was embarrassing the way I played.
"He said 'if you keep playing like that, you will quite fast go back to Germany'.
"It was bad, but I learned from it."
Gross' dad urged his son to not look for free-kicks and instead play "faster" to adapt to the Premier League.
It was to prove important advice as Gross has become a hugely popular and influential player at Brighton.
Across his two spells at the club - having returned this summer following a two-year stint at Borussia Dortmund - Gross has contributed to 87 Premier League goals, scoring 35 times and providing 52 assists, the joint-highest total of goal involvements by a German player in the competition's history.
Gross' dad was not just a parent keen to see his son make the best of his talent, but he had also been a respected football coach.
A former player, Stephan Gross built up decades of experience of coaching at youth level.
In the early 2000s he was youth team coach at VfL Neckarau, where he coached his son and helped him and several others develop impressively enough to catch the eye of professional clubs.
"He coached us from maybe from age 10 to 15," Gross said.
"But he prepared us for what it takes on a professional level - that the mental side is really important and you have to be resilient to pressure.
"Technical game, behaviour, all of those things I think he coached into not just me, but there's a lot of players [he coached] who also went on to play in the Bundesliga, or other levels."
Gross, Manuel Gulde, Robin Szarka and Marco Terrazzino all moved to TSG 1899 Hoffenheim as a result of Gross' coaching.
As is often the case, Gross has had to evolve as a player with age, and by his own admission he is a different type of player now than he was in his first stint at Brighton.
The 35-year-old is still chipping in with the goals and assists, with four of each in his 11 Premier League games so far, but now finds himself as much an on-field coach as a player.
"I try to put the gameplan on the pitch and try to drive and coach and improve my team-mates around me," he said.
"I see in other teams where players on the pitch organise the press and I think it's really important and I try to just put the gaffer's idea as a player on the pitch."
To still be going at the age he is and performing to the level he is, it is clear Gross loves football, despite having an issue that some might have thought would have curtailed his career early on - an allergy to grass.
"I have had this allergy since I was a child, but I can handle it. It's not that bad," he said.
"My mum always texts me [when there's a reaction]. She sees it straight away."

items.summary:
Uganda starts mRNA Ebola vaccine trial in first for Africa
The trial targets the less common Bundibugyo strain behind the Ebola outbreak in neighbouring DRC.
Africa’s first clinical trial has begun in Uganda of an mRNA vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain behind a deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democ
items.text:
Uganda starts mRNA Ebola vaccine trial in first for Africa
The trial targets the less common Bundibugyo strain behind the Ebola outbreak in neighbouring DRC.
Africa’s first clinical trial has begun in Uganda of an mRNA vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain behind a deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The state-run Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI) said in a statement on Friday that the trial began in collaboration with Moderna, a United States-based company which manufactures the vaccine.
The Ugandan trial is the second for the vaccine, after Moderna began its first human trial of the shots in Canada in August, targeting adults from 18 to 65 years old.
UVRI said the Ugandan trial will for the first time test the vaccine’s safety and ability to trigger an immune response in children aged 1 year and above, and aims to enrol 224 volunteers.
“Children are often among those hardest hit when Ebola strikes, yet they ‌are too often the last to benefit from new vaccines,” said Richard Hatchett, chief executive officer of the Coalition ‌for ‌Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is helping fund the vaccine.
Other options
The other potential candidate for combating the Bundibugyo strain is the ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector vaccine developed by India’s Serum Institute and the University of Oxford. It will begin testing in the DRC on Monday.
But Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which brings together government and private donors to help developing countries acquire jabs at affordable prices, is not waiting.
It signed a purchase commitment last week with the Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of ChAdOx1, and plans to have “hundreds of thousands” ready to deploy should the trials prove successful and be approved by the World Health Organization and the DRC government.
Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi’s director of global health security, said he hoped trials of the drug would conclude in early 2027 and that, if successful, the purchase deal could move up deployment by months.
On Thursday, DRC government data showed that at least 12,021 Ebola infections have been confirmed, including 5,904 deaths since the outbreak began in mid-May.
Uganda declared its Ebola outbreak over on July 28. It had recorded 20 infections and two deaths, according to the Ministry of Health.

As the artificial intelligence (AI) race between the United States and China heats up, with both superpowers vying to gain a c
items.text:
How Israel is fast-tracking data centres in bid to become ‘AI superpower’
Israel is looking to data centres to boost its data processing, military strength and global clout.
As the artificial intelligence (AI) race between the United States and China heats up, with both superpowers vying to gain a competitive edge, a third party is looking to punch above its weight.
Israel, which Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has called a “second home“, is cutting red tape and fast-tracking data centre construction to position itself as a key hub for the AI ecosystem.
“We will turn Israel into a global AI superpower,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in June, as his government announced a sweeping national plan to accelerate AI intelligence development.
Israel’s position on the AI landscape is arguably well set. US giant Nvidia began its stratospheric rise to the world’s most valuable semiconductor company with its acquisition of Mellanox, an Israeli company which supplies computer networking products, in April 2020 for nearly $7bn.
That acquisition was central to Nvidia’s success: its networking business, built around Mellanox, generated more than $21bn in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That’s about 18 percent of Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue.
Now, Nvidia’s operations in Israel are its largest in research and development outside the US. It has doubled its employees there in the past three years to 6,000 people across seven research and development centres and has plans to build a major research and development campus in Kiryat Tivon near Haifa to accommodate up to 10,000 employees.
In an interview with Israeli media in September, Netanyahu laid out an ambitious timeframe for Israel’s AI roadmap. “Within five years, we will be the third AI power,” he said.
Analysts view his infrastructure drive as a structural shift that will expand Israel’s high-speed data-processing capabilities, carrying major implications for both military strength and geopolitical influence.
A new national infrastructure
The pinnacle of Israel’s innovation drive is the planned Ofek Data Center, set to become Israel’s largest data-processing facility upon completion in the second half of 2029, north of the port of Ashdod.
Financed by a consortium including US-based digital infrastructure firm Serverfarm and the Israel Infrastructure Fund (IIF), the project is expected to cost $1.5bn initially, with an additional $5bn planned for future upgrades.
The facility will connect directly to European markets via an underwater fibre-optic cable and will integrate Nvidia data centre GPUs to accelerate server workloads, launching with a capacity of 130MW before expanding to 200MW.
Israel currently counts 67 data centres, according to research group Data Center Map, and Netanyahu’s government has been removing regulatory bottlenecks to facilitate new projects.
In February, the government launched an initiative to classify AI data centres as national infrastructure to bypass local regulation, but the rapid expansion hit a major bottleneck last month when the Israeli Electrical Authority capped the capacity of all new data centres in the country at 200MW due to high grid connection demand.
Analysts say electricity availability is the largest operating expense for modern data centres, and a key factor in determining directly how quickly new facilities can be built and what profit margins they can achieve.
“Fast-tracking permits is a governance decision,” Rajiv Dalal, a London-based independent researcher and adviser on AI governability, told Al Jazeera. “Securing the electricity to run what gets built is a governability question, and the distance between the two is where the economic case gets tested.
“Israel is small, grid-constrained and dependent on imported hardware,” Dalal said, while “superpower status requires gigawatt-level capacity, reliable power and steady access to advanced chips.”
In short, a greater AI vision requires a lot of power.
To allocate electricity to servers, Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Eli Cohen has stressed that Israel must develop nuclear energy as a power source, as well as using natural gas from the Eastern Mediterranean offshore fields Tamar, Leviathan and Karish – near disputed maritime waters with Lebanon – and a fourth, Katlan, expected to come online in 2027.
The Ofek Data Center will be directly powered by an 850MW gas-fired power station constructed adjacent to Ashdod’s port, according to Israeli media reports.
Mark Esposito, a public policy scholar at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University in the US, said the rationale for building data centres is more geopolitical and strategic than narrowly commercial.
“On pure market-efficiency grounds, domestic AI data centres are often hard to justify,” Esposito told Al Jazeera. “For a country with strategic AI ambitions, a domestic data-centre footprint is less about immediate returns and more about owning a chokepoint in the next industrial phase.”
Domestic data centres do not by themselves make a country an AI superpower, but it is very hard to become one without them. “They are the territorial anchor of AI power,” Esposito said.
Over time, these facilities “draw in cloud providers, AI labs, semiconductor packaging, cooling specialists and energy infrastructure, building an ecosystem in which talent, capital and data reinforce one another,” the analyst added.
Gaining ‘immense power’ globally
When Netanyahu’s government approved the plan to fast-track AI data centres in February, citing national security, the prime minister said the move would be a “decisive factor in the continued cultivation of our power”.
“However, it is not just about projecting or building power; it is also about gaining immense power advantages on a global scale,” he said. “We must do this because we are a small and threatened country.”
