items.title: Live: Ukraine downs Russian drone with laser technology as Moscow intercepts overnight assault
items.summary:
Live: Ukraine downs Russian drone with laser technology as Moscow intercepts overnight assault
                                                                                                    
                            Issued on: Modified:
items.text:
Live: Ukraine downs Russian drone with laser technology as Moscow intercepts overnight assault
                                                                                                    
                            Issued on: Modified: 
                                                    
                                    
                            
                                                                                                            
                            
                                        
    
        
                    
    
                                    
    
                    
                                Russia shot down 1,200 drones targeting Moscow overnight, Russian authorities said Saturday. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up their attacks using projectiles in recent months, with Ukraine confirming on Friday it had downed a Russian jet-powered drone with laser technology for the first time. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.             
                                                    
        
                    
                                    
                        Russia shoots down 1,200 Ukrainian drones in overnight assault
Russian authorities said Saturday that more than 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been shot down in a new night-time attack, with hundreds aimed at the Moscow region.
Ukraine also reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured. 
Both sides have stepped up air attacks in recent months.
More than 460 drones headed towards the Moscow area between late Friday and early Saturday, the capital's mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on the state-backed Max platform. He added that 123 were destroyed as they neared the city.
The Russian defence ministry said that air defence forces "intercepted and destroyed 1,246 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles" in more than a dozen regions including Moscow.
                                    
                        Ukraine deploys laser technology for first time to down Russian drone
Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, its state-backed defence group Brave1 told AFP on Friday. 
Earlier this week, Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, published footage showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system. 
The weapon was developed by a recipient of a Brave1 grant and operated by a private air defence team, the Brave1 team confirmed. 
But they cautioned that "a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment".
"Laser air defence remains an experimental technology," the contact said, adding at least seven teams in Ukraine were currently working on laser weapons. 
                                    
                        Growing frustrations with US – Zelensky
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed frustration with the US stance towards Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington, as new questions emerged about Europe’s future financial commitments to Ukraine.
In an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday Zelensky said he wants the US to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite US President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.

Follow along for the latest on Russia's war on Ukraine.

items.title: Explosive Fury vs Klitschko canvas row revisited
items.summary:
Tyson Fury vs Wladimir Klitschko: Revisit the furious canvas row that changed the course of the heavyweight division
On November 28 in 2015 Tyson Fury toppled the man who had dominated the heavyweight division when he beat Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf; But he almost had to scuttle the contest on
items.text:
Tyson Fury vs Wladimir Klitschko: Revisit the furious canvas row that changed the course of the heavyweight division
On November 28 in 2015 Tyson Fury toppled the man who had dominated the heavyweight division when he beat Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf; But he almost had to scuttle the contest on the day of the fight in an explosive row over the ring surface, which saw Vitali Klitschko weighing in
Thursday 26 November 2026 15:15, UK
On this day in 2015 Tyson Fury scaled his Everest. He dethroned Wladimir Klitschko, the dominant heavyweight of that era, to win the unified WBO, IBF and WBA world heavyweight championships.
It was the goal Fury had targeted throughout his career. Klitschko had ruled the division for a decade and was selling out stadiums in Germany.
Fury travelled to Dusseldorf as the underdog but utterly confident he had the tools to unravel Klitschko.
However on the day of the fight, an explosive row at the Esprit Arena threatened to scuttle the whole event.
Peter Fury, Tyson's uncle and then trainer, decided he wanted to inspect the ring in advance. Then they spotted something they hadn't expected. Feeling the canvas, they realised that the layers under it were spongy.
Tyson Fury climbed through the ropes to bounce on the balls of his feet on the canvas where he was due, a few hours later, to stage a remarkable win.
"No way you can fight on that," his father John Fury said.
"You know what they've done that for," the then heavyweight title challenger said, "so I can't move."
Speaking to the camera, Tyson Fury declared: "They must have half a foot deep of sponge on the canvas. It's like training on a beach on the sand. It's absolutely ridiculous and I can tell you now, Sky Sports viewers, there's no fight if that ring ain't sorted.
"I'm a mover and I move, that's the way I fight. I can't move in that ring."
History could have been very different. If he'd gone ahead with the fight, he could - probably would - have lost. He certainly wouldn't have been able to box in the way he did so successfully later that night.
"My fighter is not fighting in quicksand," his trainer Peter Fury declared at the time.
They undid the ring canvas to look underneath; there were two soft layers that they insisted had to be removed.
Vitali Klitschko, Wladimir's older brother and a fearsome former world heavyweight champion himself, was on hand to respond. He stood in the ring himself, towering over the top rope and glowering down at Fury's team on the floor of the arena.
Mick Hennessy, Fury's promoter, told him: "You're trying to control this but it's not in the interest of health and safety. So we need it sorted.
"Your ankle or your knee could go on this, it's too thick."
Vitali, a formidable advocate for his brother, argued fiercely, gesturing animatedly as he said: "Both fighters have the same conditions. Same gloves, same ring and you're unhappy always.
"Everything you say is excuses," he roared. "Do you want to fight or not?"
Fury's team weren't bluffing though. They were prepared to walk away.
John Fury raged at Bernd Boente, Klitschko's manager, in a corridor at the arena. He told him directly: "The fight's off, forget about it." Then he stormed off.
He later said: "If they hadn't replaced it, there wouldn't have been a fight."
Fury's team got their way. The offending layers were removed and Fury did indeed use his footwork and mobile long-range boxing to defuse Klitschko, a dangerous puncher, so adept normally at controlling distance but who just couldn't pin down an inspired Fury.
That blazing row did change the course of the heavyweight division. It was an important element in a monumental victory for the Englishman. Fury became the dominant figure in the weight class. He was unable to meet Klitschko again in a rematch; struggling with depression, he stepped away from the sport.
But Fury's mental health improved and he was able to make a famous comeback. He cemented his legend against Deontay Wilder, becoming a two-time heavyweight world champion without losing a fight.
Now he has the chance to become a three-time champion when he fights his great rival Anthony Joshua for the first time with a vacant WBA title on the line.
That climactic fight is two weeks away as Fury looks to start the final chapter in a championship story that began 11 years ago today.

items.title: Dawson: Rashid is still England's No 1 white-ball spinner
items.summary:
England T20s in Australia: Liam Dawson says Adil Rashid still No 1 spinner as tourists target series victory in Sydney
Liam Dawson has been preferred to Adil Rashid in ODIs of late but spinners play together in T20s, helping England into a 2-1 series lead over Australia with two matches left; Dawson
items.text:
England T20s in Australia: Liam Dawson says Adil Rashid still No 1 spinner as tourists target series victory in Sydney
Liam Dawson has been preferred to Adil Rashid in ODIs of late but spinners play together in T20s, helping England into a 2-1 series lead over Australia with two matches left; Dawson hails two more spinners in James Coles and Rehan Ahmed ahead of Sunday's fixture in Sydney (8.15am UK)
Saturday 28 November 2026 07:28, UK
Liam Dawson insists Adil Rashid remains England's No 1 white-ball spinner - even though he has seemingly taken the Yorkshireman's place as first-choice pick in ODIs.
Stalwart Rashid, 38, has been left out of England's last six 50-over encounters - three in Pakistan and then three in Australia - with Dawson the frontline slow bowler for those games.
The duo form a potent pairing in T20 internationals, though, and bowled economically - and in Dawson's case prolifically, as he took 3-16 from three overs - in Brisbane on Friday as England took a 2-1 lead over Australia in the five-match series.
- Jamie Overton goes 'back to basics' to deliver big England win
- Australia's Sandpapergate probe to include 2017-18 Ashes
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream contract-free with NOW
Speaking ahead of Sunday's fourth fixture in Sydney (8.15am UK), Dawson, 36, said: "I'm not sure I've knocked him out [of the team] because it's all conditions dependent, but he's still England's best white-ball spinner, without doubt," he said.
"I wouldn't look too far into what's happened on this trip, or in Pakistan before that. He'll certainly come good again because he's a world-class performer."
On his own ascent into a key player for England, Dawson said: "Having the backing of [captain Harry Brook] for the past 18 months, and to play as much as I have, has been brilliant. I've really enjoyed it and hopefully I can carry on and keep performing.
"It's obviously nice but I'm very realistic from a personal point of view. I know how good Rash is, everybody in world cricket knows how good he is."
'Ahmed has a fantastic attitude'
Dawson also hailed two more England spinners, in Sussex's James Coles, who made his debut against Australia in this T20 series, and Rehan Ahmed, who has been added to the squad for the final two fixtures following Will Jacks' trip ending early due to a broken hand.
The Hampshire bowler added: "Colesy has done so well for someone so young, I think people forget that, and he's got a hell of a lot of cricket ahead of him.
"Rehan's a great lad, I've known him a couple of years now and he's one of the hardest workers - always wants to bat, always wants to bowl, always wants to field. He's got a fantastic attitude.
"I've played a lot of cricket and I'm a lot older than those guys so I'll chat to them in training.
"You've always got to find your own way as well, work it out a little bit, but I'm very happy to speak to them both and help, of course."

items.title: Trump’s tariffs have become America’s new normal
items.summary:
Trump’s tariffs have become America’s new normal
Even a Democratic administration may struggle to reverse tariffs that help finance Trump’s tax cuts.
Markets hardly blinked at the announcement of a new series of proposed tariff schedules from United States President Donald Trump’s administration on
items.text:
Trump’s tariffs have become America’s new normal
Even a Democratic administration may struggle to reverse tariffs that help finance Trump’s tax cuts.
Markets hardly blinked at the announcement of a new series of proposed tariff schedules from United States President Donald Trump’s administration on November 25. Although the affected economies – including the European Union, China, Japan, Indonesia and Taiwan – account for more than 53 percent of US goods trade, the announcement was met with something of a whimper.
On November 25, the S&P 500 and the benchmark 10-year Treasury bond hardly moved. Compare that with the turmoil that followed Trump’s April 2, 2025, “Liberation Day” announcements. The S&P 500 fell 10.5 percent over the next two trading days, wiping some $5 trillion off its value – a record two-day loss. US Treasuries, normally a haven in times of stress, sold off alongside them as the yield on 10-year Treasuries posted its biggest weekly jump since 2001.
US markets may face volatility driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and its geoeconomics, but they no longer treat tariffs as so frightful.
That is because Trump’s tariffs have become normalised – in two senses of the word. The first is that the markets have accepted that tariffs will be a fact of life under the Trump administration.
There should be no doubt that Trump is a true believer. He told ABC: “I believe very strongly in tariffs. I believe that Japan … should pay a major tax, like a 15 or a 20 percent tax on any product they sell in the United States” – in 1989. Fifteen percent is indeed Japan’s proposed tariff rate. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.
True, Trump suffered a landslide rebuke to his economic policies and geopolitical agenda in the November 3 midterms. Democrats took both houses of Congress and flipped at least seven Senate seats – including Kansas, which had not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. But with his almost gleeful vow to become “Mr Veto”, there should be no expectation that tariffs will be swiftly overturned.
The second normalisation is in the sense that Trump and the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) are now pursuing the tariffs using far less controversial and less blunt instruments. That follows a string of defeats at the US Court of International Trade and the US Supreme Court for his broader approach of using justifications under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
Instead, the latest tariffs were proposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, at the end of an eight-month investigation into what USTR calls “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing.
Section 301 tariffs are nothing new. Ronald Reagan used them in 1987 to impose 100 percent duties on $300 million worth of Japanese electronics in a dispute over semiconductors. Bill Clinton used them in 1999 to slap 100 percent tariffs on $308 million of European goods. The prospect of them being overturned by the courts is far more remote.
Because Section 301 tariffs require an investigation into alleged unfair trade practices, complete with hearings and public comment periods, these announcements were largely priced in by the markets. Although there is much quibbling about some of the justifications USTR cited, the US courts – particularly this Supreme Court – are likely to defer to the White House even where its reasoning seems prima facie questionable.
Some of Trump’s reasoning is questionable indeed. A parallel Section 301 action, which has imposed tariffs on the EU since July, rests on the claim that the bloc has failed to implement an effective ban on imports made with forced labour, even though European rules on prison labour are considerably stricter than those in the US.
Helping ease digestion of the latest move, Trump has at least honoured the terms of agreements he made with countries such as Japan, Vietnam and the EU on capping tariff levels after his initial IEEPA tariff efforts. The proposed rates top out at 15 percent for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland, and at 20 percent for Vietnam, in line with their deals. Outside China, the new rates would not stack on top of the forced labour duties or on the Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminium, cars and other specific industries.
However, the cumulative effect of Trump’s tariffs is still stunning. They are set to lift the average US statutory tariff rate from 11.4 percent to 13.9 percent – and the rate for Mexico, the largest US trading partner after the EU, is yet to be announced. That compares with a weighted average tariff rate of just 2.3 percent when Trump returned to office in January 2025.
And Trump is clearly still willing to use tariffs as a weapon in trade disputes. USTR has floated fallback rates should talks falter: 20 percent for the EU and Japan, 25 percent for South Korea and Taiwan, and 35 percent for Vietnam.
The Section 301 investigation for China found that tariffs of up to 40 percent were “warranted”, though USTR proposed only a 20 percent tariff, albeit one that stacks on top of the Section 301 tariffs Trump imposed on China in his first term. That would give many Chinese goods a combined tariff rate of about 45 percent. This is in line with the cap agreed in the trade truce Trump negotiated with Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, and extended in September until January 10, 2027.
However, Trump is clearly signalling that if the truce is not extended again, the combined China tariff rate will go up, to as much as 65 percent. This is set to be at the heart of negotiations with Xi at the G20 summit at Trump’s Doral resort outside Miami on December 14-15.
The question is not whether tariffs, and the threat of more, will continue to be among the most frequently used tools in the Trump administration’s geoeconomic arsenal. That much is certain.
Instead, the question is how long tariffs can outlast their proponents. This is sure to be a sticking point for any Democratic pres

'It doesn't come from me' - Eckert on taunts at Boro

items.text:
'It doesn't come from me' - Eckert on taunts at Boro
- Published
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has stressed that taunts from the club aimed at Championship opponents Middlesbrough did not come from him.
Saints beat the league leaders 2-0 on Friday night, scoring twice in the second half while keeping a clean sheet in a fiery game at St Mary's.
On Friday morning, the club posted a much talked about video recalling the play-off campaign last season and how success was "ours... until it wasn't" before Middlesbrough "got another go", followed by footage of Oli McBurnie's winner for Hull at Wembley.
Eckert - who was at the centre of the Spygate scandal that led to Southampton being expelled from the play-offs in May - revealed after Friday's game that he did not like the video.
He said he had not been aware that it would be played before kick-off
Saints fans cheered as McBurnie's winner hit the back of the net on the big screens.
The match ended with the song Stop Crying Your Heart Out by Oasis ringing out as Middlesbrough's players left the field.
A box of tissues was also conveniently placed on the media conference table after the match, before Eckert removed it once made aware it was next to him.
"I just hope that we can do everything that we do with class," an exasperated Eckert said after the game.
"I hope that everyone that came here, especially the Middlesbrough staff and players, know that these things don't come from me.
"I think that everything you do in victory or defeat should be with class and I try to do that. I hope that there's an appreciation that this doesn't come from me and I'll make sure that Kim [Hellberg, Middlesbrough's head coach] knows this.
"I hope this doesn't become a big topic as the football game was so good today, I respect Kim and Middlesbrough a lot."
Tensions spilled over during the game, as former Middlesbrough player Finn Azaz ran the length of the field to celebrate in front of Boro supporters late in the game.
Supporters had to be held back as they tried to enter the field, as the Saints attacker made a crying gesture in their direction.
He later justified his celebration by sharing that it was a response to Boro fans singing about his family in games last season.
Hellberg said that he felt Azaz should have handled the situation differently.
"It's always a thing that you have as a footballer and a coach to try to be a role model," Hellberg told BBC Radio Tees.
"Be better. I know it's sometimes tough with emotions sometimes. I said to [Azaz that] it wasn't a good move.
"I know players, whatever they are, are young people and sometimes get their emotions into it, which you sometimes have to have respect for. But you can handle it and should handle it in a better way."

items.title: How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash
items.summary:
It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.
A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.
Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest g
items.text:
It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.
A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.
Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.
It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.
But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.
When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.
That was the moment when Tozzo – who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.
Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.
It was a first continental final for the Brazilian team.
"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.
Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.
"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.
Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".
The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.
The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.
A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.
"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.
"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."
To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.
At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.
Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.
A number of key details about the disaster were established early on.
- At 21:16 local time, the aircraft displayed a low fuel warning but flew on without the crew alerting local authorities.
- Fourteen minutes later, the plane began its descent to Medellin airport but was put in a holding pattern.
- At 21:49, the crew requested priority permission to land, vaguely citing "problems with fuel".
"I remember the lights went out suddenly; then I started praying, asking God to help us," recalled defender Neto, the last of the survivors to be found.
"But a lot of people thought the plane was just landing because it was not an abrupt fall."
Within five minutes, all the engines, drained of fuel, failed.
"Then, I couldn't hear the plane engine any more. It was just a wind. And then an alarm: beep beep beep," Neto told the BBC World Service in 2017.
Seven thousand kilometres away in the small southern Brazilian city of Chapeco, Tozzo watched the scale of the disaster unfold on TV screens at the stadium in the middle of the night.
"At five o'clock in the morning, the players' wives began to arrive. It was despair. People threw themselves on the ground and cried," says Tozzo, a local entrepreneur who was the club's vice-president at the time and had joined the club in 2009 when they were not even playing in Brazil's national football pyramid.
Two days earlier, Tozzo had suffered misgivings about the trip that were so strong that he had changed his mind about travelling to Medellin.
"It was a thing from God. It was not for me to go. I called [financial director] Decio, who organised all our trips, and I told him that I would not go," he says.
"He went crazy with me. 'Why? You agreed to go, now you do not want to go? You have to go.'
"My sister was next to me, saying, 'You need to go to this match, you worked so hard to get to this moment.' But in my head I said, 'No Ivan, I will not go', and I stayed at home."
After the crash, he had another strong feeling about his path.
"I think I had a mission here on Earth to continue Chapecoense after the accident," Tozzo says. "I was the only one of the directors left alive so I took over as [interim] president."
A sleepless week followed in which Tozzo arranged flights to Colombia for doctors, relatives and pastors to identify and recover the remains and be with the survivors.
A memorial service was organised and, in pouring rain, the coffins were brought into Chape's stadium, Arena Conda.
During the service came the news that Atletico Nacional had asked for the Copa Sudamericana trophy and winners' prize mo

Taiwan holds local elections under Beijing's watchful gaze

items.text:
Taiwan holds local elections under Beijing's watchful gaze
Taiwan is electing local leaders across 22 cities and counties on Saturday amid accusations by Taiwanese authorities of attempts by China to interfere and sow distrust in the island-nation’s electoral system. Chinese authorities reject the allegations.
Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election Saturday that will test whether the ruling party can notch some wins at the local level.
Polls opened at 8am and are set to close at 4pm Results normally are tallied and announced the same day. Winners will serve four-year terms.
Unlike presidential elections, when relations with China and Beijing’s pressure on the island are major issues, Saturday’s vote is focused more on local concerns, including social welfare benefits and other issues affecting people’s daily lives.
But China has not been entirely absent from the debate. Taiwanese authorities have accused Beijing of attempting to sow distrust in the island’s electoral system, allegations that Chinese authorities have rejected.
Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China's People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.
Read moreTaiwan launches annual war games as pressure from China grows
Saturday's elections feature candidates mostly from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party or the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. Traditionally, the KMT has performed well in local elections. In 2022, the DPP won in only five out of 22 localities.
Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for DPP candidates, appearing Thursday night to support his party’s mayoral candidate in Taoyuan City.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy, which Beijing claims. Ahead of its elections, its government warned the public to be vigilant of any fake claims on social media, citing continuous Chinese disinformation efforts.
The capital Taipei is traditionally a KMT stronghold, but the DPP’s mayoral candidate Puma Shen has been viewed as a strong challenger to incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an.
Other notable races are in New Taipei City and Kaohsiung. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.
A third party, the Taiwan People’s Party, is running in some smaller races and supports the KMT’s candidate in the Taipei mayoral race.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Across Taipei, colorful banners promoting each candidate blanket the otherwise dull brown and gray surfaces of buildings.
Voter Chang Li-fen went to her Taipei polling place early Saturday morning. Declining to name the candidate, she said she voted for the person she thinks will be the best for the economy.
“If the Taiwan economy is good, only then will people be able to live well,” she said. “In France and in Italy, people are protesting because of energy costs, which raised the cost of living, so I think the economy is most important.”
Candidates held rallies Friday in a last-minute bid for votes.
Puma Shen traveled in a motorcade across the city stopping for 15 minutes at a time to greet the crowds of supporters lining the street, many of whom came ahead of time to specific spots his campaign had outlined on a map.
Incumbent Chiang Wan-an held a rally with supporters at night with other KMT city council members, with his supporters waving balloons, flags and light-up sticks to cheer him on.
(FRANCE 24 with AP).

items.summary:
Elon Musk can afford a little MAGA amnesia
His failed bet on the Republicans has done nothing to diminish the bipartisan appeal of his fortune.
Following the dismal performance of the Republican Party in the United States midterm elections this month, the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, admitted
items.text:
Elon Musk can afford a little MAGA amnesia
His failed bet on the Republicans has done nothing to diminish the bipartisan appeal of his fortune.
Following the dismal performance of the Republican Party in the United States midterm elections this month, the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, admitted that he felt “pretty foolish about having spent so much money” backing Republican candidates.
The CEO of Tesla and SpaceX dropped almost $500m on elections that saw Democrats sweep Congress. Granted, this isn’t exactly “so much money” for someone whose net worth hovers in the vicinity of $820bn.
Musk furthermore took the opportunity to announce that he is not, in fact, a disciple of US President Donald Trump’s signature Make America Great Again movement: “I’m not MAGA.”
This was a curious statement, no doubt, coming from a man who in very recent history has been known to sport MAGA hats and say things like: “I’m not just MAGA. I’m dark, gothic MAGA.”
Now, however, he has ditched the MAGA hat, explaining that he is not even “sure what MAGA means”. If it happens to mean a “sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party”, he remarked, “then I certainly don’t have that”.
Anyway, who needs “blind adherence” when you already have more money than anyone else on the planet?
To be sure, Musk has backed Democrats in the past, including former presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. During his brief but dramatic breakup last year with Trump – for whose 2024 electoral victory Musk claims personal credit – various members of the Democratic camp jumped at the chance to woo Musk and his money back to their side.
And the bipartisan commitment to plutocracy is something that won’t be defeated in any US election any time soon.
After Trump reassumed power last January, Musk was granted a post at the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he promptly went about dismantling government agencies and seeing to it that masses of federal workers lost their jobs – all the while personally benefiting from his own companies’ government contracts.
In his post-MAGA political reinvention, Musk has spontaneously cast himself as “ideologically quite moderate” – which might be news to anyone who associates ideological moderation with ideas such as workers having rights and that the world should not be governed by a handful of zillionaire sociopaths.
As Jim Naureckas, editor of the New York-based outlet Fairness & Accuracy In Reporting, said to me regarding the basis of Musk’s business model: “Elon Musk has amassed unfathomable wealth by convincing people that his not very profitable companies would some day make insane profits.”
As Naureckas put it, Musk in turn used that fortune “to ally himself with the ugliest elements of national and world politics, taking an active part in the looting and corrupting of the US government”. But now that the movement Musk enthusiastically hitched his wagon to is in disgrace, “he’s frantically trying to rebrand himself” despite having been “Sieg-Heiling the second Trump inauguration” a mere two years ago.
By coincidence, Musk has determined that the Democratic governor-elect of the state of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, is “quite moderate” – just like him! – so hopefully they’ll find some way to coexist in harmonious “moderation”. Texas, of course, is where Tesla and SpaceX have their headquarters, and where Musk had thus directed a significant portion of his “pretty foolish” campaign donations to ensure continued friendly Republican dominance.
Trump, for his part, had a rather less apoplectic reaction than one might have expected to Musk apparently jumping ship, telling NBC News: “He’s a friend of mine.”
This was far more cordial, at least, than the presidential tantrum that transpired after last year’s falling-out, when Trump declared Musk “so depressed and heartbroken” at having lost his post at DOGE that he was even suffering from “Trump derangement syndrome” – whatever that means.
As for what MAGA means, Musk may claim to no longer understand the significance of the movement he aided and abetted, but Trump has it quite clear: “I mean, you have to ask—there are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”
Good to have that straightened out.
Musk is not the only grotesquely rich and influential person to distance himself from MAGA in the aftermath of the midterms. There’s also the likes of Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir – the tech firm that has been fundamental to Trump’s deportation binge and other mass abuses – who is now claiming to be a “progressive”.
But as the post-electoral rebrandings and semantic acrobatics carry on, it’s worth recalling that, MAGA or no MAGA, the US has never been a place where humane ideals have been permitted to thrive. Basic rights to healthcare, shelter, and education are converted into prohibitively expensive luxuries while the military goes about terrorising other countries willy-nilly and sending billions of dollars in charitable contributions to Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip.
Meanwhile, Elon Musk is able to throw away hundreds of millions of dollars and then shrug it off as “pretty foolish”.
According to Musk, Republican midterm losses are an indication that “American elections are not just about money”.
But the thing about plutocracy is, everything is always about money. And whatever hat Musk decides to don next is not going to change that.

items.text:
Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
November 28, 2026
Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.
"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.
He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.
Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.
Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire
Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.
A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.
Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.
"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.
The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.
This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.
Language a key hurdle
Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.
"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.
David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.
"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.
Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.
Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.
"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."
Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.
Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?
German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.
But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.
The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.
These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.
"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.
The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.
"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.
While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.
"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.
"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."
Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

items.text:
US military cloud platform reportedly hacked as Pentagon insists systems are secure
Hackers reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One platform late Friday, potentially exposing sensitive military data. The Pentagon did not specifically deny that the system had been accessed, but insists its networks remain secure amid an ongoing spate of cyber-related data incidents.
The US military on Friday denied any issues with its computer security following media reports that the Air Force's cloud based system was hacked, in what would be the latest high profile breach of US digital infrastructure in recent weeks.
Asked whether the Air Force's Cloud One platform had been hacked, the Pentagon did not specifically deny that the system had been breached.
Instead, a Defense Department official told AFP late Friday that "The Department of War's systems are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world. We will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."
"As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks," a Defense Department official said earlier on Friday.
NBC News, a major US broadcaster, reported Friday citing an unnamed US official, that the cloud platform had been breached and that an attack "could have exposed sensitive military information."
The breach was first reported by Reuters earlier Friday.
Federal News Network, which specialises in covering US federal agencies, also confirmed the breach, citing a "person familiar with the incident."
The contractors discovered the hack earlier in the year while doing maintenance on the system, Federal News said.
The reported attack is the latest in a string of major outages in US government and private-sector digital infrastructure.
In recent weeks the CIA and FBI were also reportedly subject to hacks.
Suppliers for major American financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard were also hit.
In other instances, such as a major Microsoft Outlook outage, a separate US air traffic control issue and a reported issue with a top-secret National Security Agency (NSA) network earlier this month, officials were at pains to blame the outages on maintenance or defects – not intrusions.
The attacks and outages are not limited to the United States.
The European Commission last week said it came under an AI-assisted cyberattack in October.
AFP was hit by a cyber attack on Thursday, forcing a major client-facing system to be taken offline.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP).

items.title: The USWNT is going to the World Cup. Now the real work begins
items.summary:
MANSFIELD, Texas -- Lindsey Heaps was not going to talk about the 2027 Women's World Cup. Not until her team, the United States, had officially clinched a berth.
Less than 36 hours later, that job was complete: The U.S. women's national team emphatically defeated El Salvador 8-0 in the Concacaf W Ch
items.text:
MANSFIELD, Texas -- Lindsey Heaps was not going to talk about the 2027 Women's World Cup. Not until her team, the United States, had officially clinched a berth.
Less than 36 hours later, that job was complete: The U.S. women's national team emphatically defeated El Salvador 8-0 in the Concacaf W Championship quarterfinals on Friday at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium to qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup.
Ashley Sanchez set the pace with a first-half hat trick. Her three goals came less than seven minutes apart, making it one of the fastest hat tricks in team history.
Now, the more difficult work truly begins.
The U.S. has now qualified for all 10 Women's World Cups, winning four of them. The Americans' worst finish in program history came at the previous edition, in 2023, and a largely overhauled group of players hopes it can restore glory to the program next year in Brazil. U.S. head coach Emma Hayes has overturned and refined both the roster and the team's tactics since taking the job in late 2023.
Friday's result felt like such a foregone conclusion to the world that Jamaica's acting coach, Deon Burton, repeatedly spoke in his postgame news conference about preparing for the USWNT in the semifinal even though it was yet to be confirmed as the opponent for Jamaica, which won Friday's first quarterfinal to qualify for the 2027 World Cup.
That confirmation came quickly and emphatically. It took about 30 minutes for the floodgates to open. The U.S. scored seven goals in a first half for the third time in program history, and El Salvador failed to put a shot on goal. The U.S. completed nearly five times as many passes as El Salvador.
Granted, all of that was expected. The U.S. is the second-ranked team in the world, four-time World Cup champion and five-time (and reigning) Olympic champion. El Salvador is ranked No. 78 in the world and was playing in its first Concacaf W Championship match.
Still, Hayes has been demanding more efficiency from her team in front of goal no matter the opponent, and she at least got that in the first half Friday. Even if the process often felt like a training exercise for U.S. players, the onus was still on them to do what everyone expected and to do it in a big way. They did that.
Sanchez bagged a hat trick, jumping on the opportunity to start with forward Trinity Rodman ruled out of the tournament due to a recent shoulder injury. Sanchez, the 2026 NWSL MVP, also scored in her previous game, against world No. 1 Spain.
The U.S. also stayed patient and broke down El Salvador's attempt at staying compact defensively. That patience and creativity has not always been a given throughout the years.
So, as much as there is an asterisk on this result in that the opponent did not pose a great challenge, Hayes will still have seen some progress in areas where she has demanded it. She and her players can also now start talking about the 2027 World Cup in a real way, rather than adding the caveat that they still must qualify.
With the obvious and expected result out of the way, the U.S. women can officially turn their attention to Brazil.
"We have been talking openly, honestly about this game for a long time," U.S. midfielder Sam Coffey told reporters on Friday, saying that qualifying was the first "box to check" on a road map that the team has long stared at.
The next, most immediate box to check is finishing the job and winning the Concacaf W Championship. On Dec. 11, the U.S. women will learn their three group-stage opponents at the World Cup draw.
More challenging matches await the U.S. in its preparation in the coming months. The U.S. must show this kind of ruthless efficiency against better opponents, which has not consistently happened in recent years by Hayes' own criticisms of her squad.
The Americans will also continue to be challenged by injury issues that have prevented Hayes from truly having a preferred XI on the field. Rodman's latest injury adds to that list, and defender Naomi Girma's ongoing calf injury struggles could be a real make-or-break for the U.S. next year. Girma is arguably the world's best defender when healthy.
And no matches will have better prepared the U.S. than its pair of grueling, physical away matches against Brazil in June, or its two recent games against Spain in which the U.S. was technically outclassed.
Now, at least, the U.S. can talk about the World Cup without feeling like it is violating some unspoken law of the universe. The U.S. is heading to the 2027 World Cup, and the only acceptable outcome is to win it.

items.title: USWNT player ratings: Ashley Sanchez a 10/10 as Americans seal World Cup place
items.summary:
The U.S. women's national team earned a dominant 8-0 win against El Salvador on Friday in a Concacaf W Champions Cup quarterfinal match at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Mansfield that secured qualification for next year's World Cup.
Following a fairly competitive start, the U.S. quickly took cha
items.text:
The U.S. women's national team earned a dominant 8-0 win against El Salvador on Friday in a Concacaf W Champions Cup quarterfinal match at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Mansfield that secured qualification for next year's World Cup.
Following a fairly competitive start, the U.S. quickly took charge with goals from Kennedy Wesley, Tierna Davidson, Mallory Swanson, Sophia Wilson and a hat trick from Ashley Sanchez in a rapid-fire first half. After the break, the U.S. continued its attacking pressure but weren't able to find the back of the net once again until the 80th minute when Croix Bethune made it 8-0.
With the one-sided result in hand, the U.S. will face Jamaica on Tuesday in the semifinal stage of the Concacaf W Champions Cup.
Manager rating (out of 10)
Emma Hayes, 10 -- What could you fault or criticize in this outstanding result? Maybe we could note the U.S. still trying to move through the bunker within the first 30 minutes that included just one goal against the underdogs, but that feels foolish to write in such a significant victory for Hayes. In what looked like a 4-2-4 formation, it was an effective and efficient performance for Hayes and her players.
Player ratings (0-10; 10 = best; 5 = average)
GK Claudia Dickey, 8 -- Not much work to do, but was still involved in the buildup of a few plays going forward. A clean sheet is still a clean sheet.
DF Emily Fox, 8 -- Earned the hockey assist for Wesley's goal, as well as one for Sanchez. Looks dangerous going forward.
DF Kennedy Wesley, 9 -- Scored the game-opening goal and looked comfortable in the backline throughout the match. An excellent performance, and she connected well with Davidson.
DF Tierna Davidson, 9 -- Like Wesley, Davidson was confident defensively and also provided a first-half goal.
DF Gisele Thompson, 8 -- No goals or assists to her name but credit the fullback who was a menace with her aggressive runs on the left flank that helped create a number of dangerous opportunities. Also hit the woodwork late.
MF Lindsey Heaps, 9 -- The captain helped take charge of the center of the pitch with two assists and a hockey assist. A standout conductor of the ball alongside Lily Yohannes.
MF Lily Yohannes, 9 -- Yohannes was such a clever and creative member of the XI with her decision-making and perfectly timed passes. Earned a hockey assist for Sanchez's third goal. Great pass.
MF Ashley Sanchez, 10 -- Hat trick of goals, enough said.
FW Mallory Swanson, 10 -- Won the foul that led to her assist for Davidson's goal, secured a goal of her own and was also involved with the buildup of an additional goal. Highly involved in the attack.
FW Sophia Wilson, 10 -- A hat trick of assists and a goal of her own, that's a perfect performance for a striker.
FW Alyssa Thompson, 9 -- Drifted over to the right flank and was threatening with her two assists in the first half.
Substitutes (players introduced after 70 minutes get no rating)
FW Jaedyn Shaw, 7 -- Active in the final third, but still an alternate national team player at this moment.
MF Croix Bethune, 8 -- Scored the final goal of the night and closed the one-sided triumph.
DF Avery Patterson, 7 -- Not much work for the player who wasn't counted on making too many attacking efforts.
FW Michelle Cooper, 7 -- Limited time in the closing minutes for the USWNT, nothing too noteworthy.
MF Sam Coffey, 7 -- Helped close the big victory in the midfield.

items.summary:
El Nino-linked deluges flood cities in Peru, Ecuador
Heavy rains affect 2,000 families in Peru’s Piura and 47,000 people in Ecuador, where 34 deaths have been reported.
Several cities in Peru and Ecuador are facing major flooding after downpours in the region linked to an exceptionally strong El Nin
items.text:
El Nino-linked deluges flood cities in Peru, Ecuador
Heavy rains affect 2,000 families in Peru’s Piura and 47,000 people in Ecuador, where 34 deaths have been reported.
Several cities in Peru and Ecuador are facing major flooding after downpours in the region linked to an exceptionally strong El Nino.
In the city of Piura, capital of the Piura region in northern Peru, waist-high water filled the streets following 12 hours of heavy rains that began on Thursday.
Some 2,000 families have been affected by the rains in Piura, according to preliminary reports, National Institute of Civil Defense chief Luis Vasquez told the RPP radio station.
“This is just the first heavy rain from the El Nino phenomenon and look at how it’s treating us,” said resident Pierre Garavito, as a refrigerator bobbed in the water inside his home in Piura’s Santa Margarita neighbourhood.
“I’ve lost everything … This is how all the residents in the neighbourhood are,” he said.
Floodwaters forced authorities to relocate patients from the ward for respiratory infections at Piura’s Jose Cayetano Heredia Hospital to its auditorium. Patients in more serious condition were transferred to intensive care.
The flooding also affected the Plaza de Armas in central Piura, along with many businesses and public buildings.
Peru’s armed forces have deployed personnel and pumping equipment to remove accumulated water from the affected neighbourhoods.
Some residents, however, complained of delays with the pumping operation, with some machines reportedly stopping due to a lack of fuel.
Peru’s National Meteorology and Hydrology Service warned that moderate to heavy rainfall could continue in parts of the region over the following four days.
The Peruvian navy blamed El Nino for heavy ocean swells that recently damaged infrastructure along the country’s Pacific coast and forced the temporary closure of dozens of ports.
Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori postponed a trip to Colombia to deal with the crisis and said she plans to travel to the affected areas.
In Ecuador, the National Secretariat for Risk Management reported on Friday that 34 people had died and 47,000 had been affected by heavy rains linked to El Nino across the country.
In the western city of Manta, residents waded through chest-deep water and floated on mattresses after two rivers broke their banks.
“We’ve been soaking in mud for four days,” said Fernanda Navarrete, who lost furniture, clothes and appliances.
“To top it all off, the sewers burst; the stench is awful,” she said.
Peru and neighbouring Ecuador are among several Latin American countries that have declared national emergencies because of El Nino.
The natural phenomenon involves a rise in sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, causing worldwide changes in wind and rain patterns.
This year’s episode is projected to be the strongest on record and has already been linked to severe weather across the continent and beyond.
On Friday, United Nations agencies said hunger was set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme weather events, including El Nino.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) have warned that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen face the greatest danger.

items.text:
UN chief frontrunner urged to speak out over Albanese detention
Albanese’s detention poses a test to Costa Rica’s candidate, Rebeca Grynspan, who has led the UN’s recent straw poll.
More than 400 people have signed an open letter urging Costa Rica’s candidate to lead the United Nations, Rebeca Grynspan, to speak out after her government denied entry to UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory Francesca Albanese.
In an open letter published by the Costa Rican news outlet SURCOS Digital on Friday, signatories urged UN secretary-general frontrunner Grynspan to press Costa Rica to admit Albanese, who is being held for a second night at an airport near San Jose.
The signatories asked Grynspan to implore the Costa Rican government to “reconsider its decision, allow Francesca Albanese to enter the country and guarantee her rights to freedom of expression”.
“We believe that the independence of someone aspiring to hold the position of Secretary General is also expressed in their ability to defend the principles of the Organization when these are compromised by actions of the very State that promotes their candidacy,” said the letter, spearheaded by Juliana Martinez Franzoni, a professor at the University of Costa Rica.
UN human rights chief Volker Turk has already urged Costa Rica to reconsider.
Grynspan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The call puts Grynspan, a former Costa Rican vice president who now heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), in the spotlight at a critical moment. She led the November 20 Security Council straw poll to succeed Antonio Guterres as UN secretary-general, though two veto-wielding members opposed her candidacy in that round of secret voting.
As Grynspan, 70, vies for the top job, member states will be watching whether and how she responds after the government backing her candidacy barred a UN expert from entering the country.
The race has already drawn scrutiny of another candidate, the United Arab Emirates’ Lana Nusseibeh, over her defence of her government’s position on Sudan.
Earlier this month, Grynspan told Al Jazeera: “The UN must become less risk-averse. Its biggest risk today is the risk of not trying.”
“I have listened to people who need the UN but increasingly doubt it can act. They want leadership willing to take risks for peace,” she added.
If Grynspan secures the top UN job, she will become the first woman and the first person of Jewish descent to hold the post of UN secretary-general.

items.title: ‘Last local militant’: India declares victory but Kashmir’s rebels adapt
items.summary:
‘Last local militant’: India declares victory but Kashmir’s rebels adapt
Analysts say that shifting tactics, names and geography challenge claims of win against Kashmir’s separatist movement.
Kulgam and Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir – After a seven-day search, Indian security forces trapped
items.text:
‘Last local militant’: India declares victory but Kashmir’s rebels adapt
Analysts say that shifting tactics, names and geography challenge claims of win against Kashmir’s separatist movement.
Kulgam and Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir – After a seven-day search, Indian security forces trapped Mohammad Lateef Bhat in a mosque in Zangalpora village, in Indian-administered Kashmir’s Kulgam district.
A gunfight broke out and Bhat was killed on November 18. Described as a commander of the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), a Pakistan-based armed group, Bhat was accused of having shot at soldiers of India’s Central Reserve Police Force a week earlier with another fighter. Three soldiers were injured. His associate was also killed in the days after that attack.
But it was Bhat’s death that grabbed national headlines.
Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, the country’s second-most powerful person after Prime Minister Narendra Modi, told a public gathering that Bhat had been the last local armed fighter before he was killed.
“This development marks a significant change in the security situation in the [Kashmir] valley. It is a matter of pride for us,” Shah said. “No Kashmiri youth is currently involved in terrorist activities in the valley.”
Jammu and Kashmir police also claimed that it was the first time since the armed rebellion against Indian rule in Kashmir began in 1989 that the LeT had no local fighters.
But analysts and former security officials say the armed conflict has not gone away but merely changed form.
They point to armed groups operating under new names, the rise of operatives who remain outside official militant lists, a growing reliance on foreign fighters and encrypted communications, and a geographic shift of violence from the Kashmir valley towards the forests of Jammu in the south.
Israr Khan, a former deputy inspector general of the Jammu and Kashmir police, described Bhat’s killing as a significant victory for security forces and a major setback for LeT. But he said armed fighters could remain active without appearing in official police records.
“Through my experience, I can say he certainly is not the last militant because there are militants who are active but are not in police records,” Khan told Al Jazeera.
‘Hybrid militants’
Khan was referring to what police call “hybrid militants”, a term that emerged in Kashmir around 2020 to describe people whom security forces say carry out attacks while remaining outside official lists of known militants.
The term gained wider prominence in 2021 after police described “terrorists disguised as civilians” and “part-time terrorists”. Security officials said such individuals could remain in contact with militant groups through digital devices, receive local training and carry out attacks before returning to their normal lives, making them difficult for security agencies to detect.
Security analysts at the time suggested that the emergence of hybrid militants could reflect a change in militant strategy. Rather than openly recruiting fighters or publicly displaying weapons, militant groups could use people who maintained an outwardly normal civilian life, making them less visible to security agencies.
But the label itself has been questioned. Some analysts and rights activists argue that authorities have not clearly defined who qualifies as a hybrid militant and that the term could sometimes be applied to people previously described as militant sympathisers – or in effect, to portray every Kashmiri as a potential threat.
There is also no single official cumulative figure for people arrested as hybrid militants in Kashmir. Instead, the Jammu and Kashmir Police and other security agencies have reported arrests in individual operations.
For Khan, the existence of such fighters makes it difficult to establish whether Bhat was truly the last local militant operating in the valley. “The next five to six months are crucial and everything will become clear,” he said, cautioning that new attacks in Kashmir traced to local youth could force a reassessment.
New names
Beyond so-called hybrid fighters, Indian security forces acknowledge that they have been challenged by shapeshifting armed groups in recent years. The Resistance Front (TRF) and the People’s Anti-Fascist Front (PAFF) are armed groups operating in Indian-administered Kashmir. Both emerged after India revoked the region’s special constitutional status in August 2019.
TRF claimed responsibility for the 2025 attack on civilians in Pahalgam, Indian-administered Kashmir, when gunmen killed 26 people. India blamed Pakistan for the attack, which set the stage for the four-day war between the South Asian neighbours in May that year.
Security agencies and counterterrorism analysts regard TRF and PAFF as proxy organisations linked to established Pakistan-based armed groups. They say the groups were formed to obscure those affiliations, project a localised narrative and deflect international scrutiny, including monitoring by bodies such as the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).
For analysts, the emergence of such fronts illustrates how armed groups have adapted to a changed security environment.
Noor Ahmad Baba, a political scientist and former professor at the University of Kashmir, said claims had been made previously of local fighters no longer joining armed groups, yet attacks had continued intermittently in Jammu and Kashmir.
“Claims of Kashmir being militancy-free were made after 2019 as well,” Baba told Al Jazeera. “I am not suggesting that such a possibility is ruled out. Anything is possible, but an analysis of the ground realities presents a different picture.”
He said this did not mean there had been no improvement in the security situation on the ground. But analysts say that while local recruitment in Kashmir might be down, armed violence could be finding a new home to the south, in Jammu.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patr
items.text:
Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
- Published
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.
Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.
Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

items.text:
Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
- Published
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.
Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.
The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.
Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.
However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.
Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.
Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.
Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

items.title: Columbus Crew eliminate Messi and Inter Miami from MLS playoffs with stoppage-time strike
items.summary:
Inter Miami’s quest to defend their MLS Cup title is over.

items.text:
Inter Miami’s quest to defend their MLS Cup title is over.
The South Florida side had two gilt-edged chances to take the lead in Game 2 of their best-of-three first-round series against Columbus in the MLS Playoffs on Friday, but missed both of them along with several others, later succumbing to a terrific stoppage-time winner from Santi Rodríguez in a 1-0 win for the Crew.
The Crew’s win followed a 3-0 domination of Miami away from home at Nu Stadium, a game in which Miami defender Gonzalo Luján was issued a red card in the 36th minute. Miami’s status as MLS’s best team away from home gave them plenty of hope going into the all-important matchup in Ohio. The chances came – for Messi in the 14th minute, and a point-blank effort from Germán Berterame in the 84th that went over the bar – but the goals didn’t.
Instead, Rodríguez’s strike saw the Crew move on to the delight of a raucous home crowd in cold, rainy conditions. They will face the winner of the New England Revolution and Philadelphia Union’s matchup, with the Revs currently up 1-0 on Philly, who are hosting Game 2.
For Columbus, the result is the latest in a stunning rise from dead last in the Eastern Conference earlier this year, a start that cost head coach Henrik Rydström his job halfway through. The Crew have been on fire under interim head coach Laurent Courtois, winning eight of their final nine games to sneak into the playoffs and now two straight against the defending champions. The September acquisition of Rodríguez has been a big part of that turnaround, with the Uruguayan scoring three times and adding eight assists in the regular season.
For Miami, the focus in the aftermath a playoff exit will have global resonance thanks to Messi, who turned 39 over the summer and has already retired internationally for Argentina. This year has been a trying one for the Argentine, with his father, Jorge, suffering from a serious illness throughout the World Cup, and dying weeks after the final that Argentina lost, 1-0, to Spain.
Jorge Messi was deeply involved in his son’s footballing career, acting as his agent and closest confidant throughout.
“I wanted to win [the World Cup] to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn’t; my legs wouldn’t give any more,” Messi wrote in an open letter to his father after his passing. “I have only played football and now I have quite a few doubts about whether I’ll keep doing it for much longer.”
Messi announced his international retirement from Argentina not long after. He has not, however, indicated publicly in any way that he plans to end his playing career altogether.
Messi signed a contract extension with Miami through the 2028 MLS season late last year, but it’s unknown how the league’s change to a fall-to-spring calendar, confirmed weeks after Messi put pen to paper, will affect the deal. Regardless, Messi would be far from the first player to retire in the middle of a recently signed extension. Jordi Alba signed an extension with Miami midway through the 2025 MLS season, only to retire after winning MLS Cup last year.
If Friday’s game was Messi’s last as a professional, it will count as a disappointing one for reasons beyond the result. The Argentine was unable to produce the moments of magic that have defined so much of his career, often swarmed by Columbus defenders when he got the ball and harried by them off of it. He was responsible for one of the two biggest missed chances of the match for Miami, doing well to bring down a lofted ball within the six-yard box but firing uncharacteristically wide past the far post in the 14th minute.
Should he choose to keep playing, he’ll have plenty of reason: Miami’s regular season has earned them a spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup, one of vanishingly few trophies he has not won at the clubs he’s played for.
