items.title: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament
items.summary:
A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.
Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party mem
items.text:
A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.
Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.
“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico.
She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.
The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.
The US state department did not immediately return a request for comment.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.
Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.
Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.
The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.
Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.
Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.
“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”
Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.
“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV.
Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

items.text:
Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good as he and Adrian Lewis are knocked out of MODUS Super Series
Phil Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018; he came out of retirement for this week's MODUS Super Series International Pairs, teaming up with friend Adrian Lewis; the Pair finished second-bottom in group C and were knocked out of the event
Friday 27 November 2026 20:51, UK
Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good and has no plans to come out of retirement again.
The 16-time world champion was lured back to the oche for this year's MODUS Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth alongside his long-time friend Adrian Lewis.
The English duo lost all five of their matches on Thursday but rebounded on Friday, winning three and losing two matches, to finish second-bottom in the Group C standings.
- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results, schedule
- Luke Littler faces nightmare route at World Championship
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Taylor, 67, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after winning his final world crown, and when asked if he would make another comeback, the 14-time PDC World Championship winner told Pluto TV: "[This is] proper retirement."
A heartwarming moment unfolded after Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-3 in their final group match against Scotland, as each of the other nations arrived to give Taylor a guard of honour, as he walked away from the oche.
"I mean I'm 67, I get my pension next February," Taylor said, when asked if this would be his last competitive appearance. "I'm a pensioner now, officially!"
"I'll still do personal appearances, more having a chat with people, talking about my career, that kind of thing."
Taylor and Lewis, who teamed up to win four World Cup of Darts titles between 2012 and 2016, finished Thursday at the bottom of Group C. Friday started poorly for the Englishmen, losing to Denmark's Ivan Springborg-Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jørgensen 4-2.
Speaking on his retirement U-turn this week, Taylor said: "I was dreading it to be honest with you because I know I wasn't playing like I can do, but now I've been here and it's all over, I've loved it."
The pair hit back on Friday with a 4-3 win against Germany, then beat Switzerland and Sweden, both 4-2.
The Englishmen would tie Scotland at three legs apiece in his final competitive match, before Taylor missed a checkout for 48 for victory, in what would have been a fairy-tale finish.
"Looking back now, it's like it never happened," Taylor said, reflecting on his glittering career.
"I've said to other people who have been on stage and retired: 'How do you feel now?'
"'It's like you've never been there'. It's ever so weird. And you come up on YouTube and you just go: "No, I know. I know I was there, but I can't remember it."
"It's very, very strange because, mentally-wise, you move on. That was your former life and now my life is different."
Instead of flying around the world competing, Taylor says retirement has allowed him to spend more time with his grandchildren.
"I've got 11 grandchildren," Taylor said. "So I spend a lot of time with them now.
"[I do] things I've never done before. Go to bed when I want; I go to bed early. For me, 9pm would be like, I'd be asleep two hours before 9pm, and it's great.
"I love getting up early as well. We can do all the chores. We can go shopping and get everything done, and it isn't even 11am. It's great!
"People say I'm the GOAT [Greatest of All Time]-I'm an old goat now!"

items.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
items.summary:
'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring perform
items.text:
'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather 
  - Published1 day ago
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."
Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.
“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.
"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."
Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

items.title: Why have things started to go wrong for Manchester City under Enzo Maresca?
items.summary:
The guilty verdict
This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went
items.text:
The guilty verdict
This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling. Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory (3-2 over Ipswich, six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. City have appealed against the ruling, saying they are “innocent of the accusations”.
A faulty back four has missed O’Reilly
Nico O’Reilly’s stop-start season (four matches missed and three very short substitute appearances) has been a definite minus for the Maresca project because here is a muscular defender who offers pace, guile via a schemer’s ability to wander infield and unpick defences (he was a No 10 as a youth) and a goal threat. City conceded two in the first half without him in their 3-1 defeat at Nottingham Forest, before he came on. As a unit the defence is vulnerable, with Rúben Dias’s lack of pace and Marc Guéhi’s erratic displays key in the concerning leaking of goals.
The goalkeeper
Gianluigi Donnarumma has also been unreliable, with mistakes against Leipzig, Aston Villa and Paris Saint-Germain costing goals and points. The goalkeeper may also feel he should have stopped Rasmus Højlund’s opener in Tuesday’s 2-2 draw with Napoli. “I’m not worried about Gigio’s performance or form, knowing he has made some mistakes,” says Maresca, who has no credible competitor to the No 1 after James Trafford’s sale to Leeds in the last window. This points to a wider worry regarding questionable squad building that might not have occurred if Txiki Begiristain were still City’s director of football. His replacement, Hugo Viana, is not proving as shrewd in the market.
Is Viana a best-in-class director of football?
The Portuguese, who worked alongside Begiristain from April 2025, before taking over that summer, has made 18 signings: Enzo Fernández (£125m), Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81.3m), Antoine Semenyo (£62.5m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Tijjani Reijnders (£46.3m), Allan (£32m), Rayan Aït-Nouri (£31m), Rayan Cherki (£30.45m), Trafford (£27m), Donnarumma (£26m), Mathys Detourbet (£21.5m), Guéhi (£20m), Sverre Nypan (£12.5m), Jeremy Monga (£10m), Pierce Charles (£3m), Marcus Bettinelli (£2m), and Gerónimo Rulli (£1m). Before any add-ons, the cost is already more than an eye-watering £700m, yet, to date, only Anderson, Cherki and Ndiaye can be counted as unadulterated successes, with the form of Guéhi, Semenyo and Fernández dipping, and Bouaddi appearing promising. This leaves 10 players who have left, disappointed or must prove their potential, plus a back-up goalkeeper.
A shaky midfield
Maresca’s engine room has Anderson, a fine player but no Rodri (is anyone?), and Fernández, who is not a No 8, more a quasi-10 without Cherki’s sorcery in the position. Fernández’s role is akin to being Maresca’s on-field enforcer, the Italian having signed him from Chelsea after their time there together. Bouaddi, the main other midfielder, has impressed but is 19 so these are very early days for him, and with O’Reilly an auxiliary option and Mateo Kovacic seemingly in a bit-part role, City’s options hardly bulge. “We are trying different solutions,” Maresca says. “Last game [against Napoli] we started with Enzo, Ayyoub and Elliot. They were quite good, especially off the ball, and no doubt we’re going to find the right balance.”
The Haaland poser
Is the team totem and goal glutton happy? He was certainly glum post-Napoli, and has been spied gesticulating angrily during games. Maresca says: “Erling is a winner. It’s normal that he’s not happy when he’s not winning games but don’t forget a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch [after the Carabao Cup win against Brighton]. Erling is upset just like I am upset.” The question, though, is more of the existential kind regarding whether the Norwegian may debate a future away from City. Haaland signed a 10-year contract in January 2025 but this will mean zero should he wish to move on. If the appeal is lost and City are demoted a division (or worse), Haaland – and others – will surely depart.
Maresca – and his tactics
All factors cited have to be nullified/solved by Maresca. Settling on a first XI while addressing a tactical blueprint that has a prevailing sluggishness with the odd flash of directness – Haaland’s winner in September against Coventry, for example, came via a quick Fernández pass to Semenyo, whose cross was converted – would help. On Friday Maresca offered a flat “no” when asked whether he may change his style. He also offered an explanation for the poor displays: “It’s easy to understand – because we are four months together. Transition requires time. Probably because we won eight games in a row [from the season’s start] people were thinking here there is no transition, but I’m not a magician. We have eight or nine new players, the manager is new – you need time. No panic at all. I understand we need to win games because it is a business.”

Is Iraq facing renewed instability?
Roughly 20 percent of Iraq’s oil reserves are in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

items.text:
Israel kills four in Gaza as Hamas chief al-Hayya’s son survives strike
Four of Khalil al-Hayya’s other sons were previously killed by Israeli forces, according to the Palestinian group.
A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.
The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the strip killed four Palestinians, despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed over a year ago.
Izzeldeen al-Hayya, 29, and his family survived the Israeli strike at dawn, said Hamas official Basem Naim. Hamas sources told the Reuters news agency that several relatives were wounded, including the daughter-in-law of the Hamas chief.
The family of another of Khalil al-Hayya’s deceased sons, Azzam, also survived.
Naim described Izzeldeen as the Hamas leader’s last surviving son. Four of his brothers were killed by Israeli forces: Hamza in 2008, Osama in 2014, Humam in September last year and Azzam in May this year.
Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Humam, who was killed in an Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year. Khalil al-Hayya narrowly escaped that attack during negotiations. He was named leader of Hamas in July.
Hamas condemned Friday’s attack, describing it as an attempt to “assassinate” al-Hayya’s son and target his family.
The group linked the attack to threats made against its leader by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and accused Israel of seeking to undermine the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Hamas said the “cowardly act” exposes the “complete detachment from human and moral values” of Israeli leaders.
Continued Israeli attacks in Gaza
Deadly Israeli attacks continued elsewhere in Gaza on Friday.
A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in a drone att on a vehicle in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.
Wafa named the victim as Khaled Assaf and quoted witnesses as saying a vehicle was struck in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp.
In the southern city of Rafah, Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of three Palestinians and rescued two wounded people following an attack near Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, Wafa reported.
Israeli army gunfire injured a Palestinian child in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
Medical sources and witnesses told Wafa that Israeli forces repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced people in the area from their positions near the eastern “Yellow Line”.
Friday’s attacks followed a series of Israeli raids on Thursday that killed 10 Palestinians, including a senior education official.
Israel’s ‘incitement against hospitals’
Also on Friday, Hamas described as “ridiculous” the Israeli army’s claim that it used one of the buildings at Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza City as an interrogation centre.
The Israeli military and Shin Bet made the allegations on Thursday, claiming Hamas was conducting military activities within the hospital complex.
The Israeli claim “comes as part of the ongoing incitement against hospitals in the Gaza Strip”, Hamas said in a statement.
Hospitals are “public places open to all civil and UN institutions operating in the enclave”, it noted, adding that Israel had never provided evidence to substantiate any of its claims.
The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which oversees the hospital, said it had no knowledge of any secret interrogation centre on the premises.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the October 2025 “ceasefire” since it took effect have killed at least 1,705 Palestinians and wounded 6,163. Israel has killed at least 74,772 Palestinians in Gaza since the genocidal war began in October 2023.

2 min: Fofana scuffs a pass upfield. Delap intercepts and spins, taking a whack from distance. Straight at Martinez. Not the best start from Fofana, who has been woefully out of form for some time now.
Forest get the game started. What to expect? Well, Forest have only scored nine goals in their 11 matches. That’s a rate of 0.82 goals per game; given their season’s xG per 90 is 1.58, that return is even poorer than it looks at first glance. Chelsea’s xG per 90 by contrast is 1.32, but they’ve scored 20 times at a rate of 1.82 per match. Something has to give, except it might not.
The teams are out! Nottingham Forest wear Garibaldi red, Chelsea third-choice white with red pinstripe. A nicely oiled Friday-night atmosphere at the City Ground, the air filled with mist rolling in from the Trent light rain. We’ll be off in a minute or two.
Xabi Alonso talks to Sky. “We want to show a good reaction from the last game … the proper fundamentals to compete … it is not just the defenders, it is the whole team … we are expecting an intense game … good atmosphere … we need to show we can compete at this level … today we need strong characters … big personalities … players on the bench ready to have a good impact … the game will be close … tight … we need to be aware of the small details … the next game is the best opportunity and we approach in that way today.”
A cheery Oliver Glasner speaks to Sky Sports. “I always felt the backing of the owner … we have constant talks … always in direct contact … assessing what’s going well and not going well … discussing how we improve things … we are very honest … we are not pleased with the season so far … we wanted to have more points … the running standard will increase … the players are working hard during the week … we are competitive in the running … it needs a good structure … it is possible to beat Chelsea, like Leeds have shown last week … it is the first opportunity [Igor Jesus and Liam Delap] play together … both have different strengths … we need to score more goals, that is clear … nine goals from 11 rounds is not satisfying.”
Here’s how the Premier League table looks as we all barrel towards one-third-of-the-season territory. Chelsea can go fifth with a win tonight, and would be guaranteed to stay there for at least 19 hours, by which point we’ll know the fate of Brentford at Manchester United, and the outcome of the Leeds-Coventry 1987 FA Cup semi-final rematch). Nottingham Forest can rise as high as 14th with victory, but their rubber-stamped 19-hour stay will only extend if Leeds beat Coventry, in which case they’re guaranteed another two-and-a-half hours, after which all would be dependent on Ipswich’s result against Aston Villa. I’ll level with you, I’m killing time until kick-off.
Jamie Carragher and Toby Alderweireld eviscerated Chelsea’s defence earlier this week on Monday Night Football. Xabi Alonso seems to have taken that criticism seriously, because by the looks of it, he’s dropped Levi Colwill and replaced him in the centre of defence by Moisés Caicedo, with Jordan Henderson deputising for the Ecuadorian in midfield. That’s a ballsy call, given that Chelsea’s midfield crumbled to a premium grade of dust when Caicedo was injured against Leeds. At least he’ll still be on the pitch this time.
Chelsea make three changes to their starting team, in the wake of that 1-4 home skelping by Leeds. Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Pedro Neto are in; Levi Colwill, Emmanuel Emegha and Estêvão drop to the bench.
Forest make two changes to their starting XI following their 2-0 defeat at Bournemouth last weekend. Igor Jesus and Xaver Schlager replace Dan Ndoye and captain Ryan Yates, who both drop to the bench.
The teams
Nottingham Forest: Sels, Jair Cunha, Milenkovic, Murillo, Munoz, McAtee, Schlager, Williams, Igor Jesus, Gibbs-White, Delap.
Subs: John Victor, Diomande, Sangare, Hudson-Odoi, Wood, Ndoye, Kalimuendo, Yates, Netz.
Chelsea: Martinez, Acheampong, Fofana, Lavia, Chavarria, Henderson, Caicedo, Pedro Neto, Palmer, Rogers, Welbeck.
Subs: Penders, Palestra, Barco, Colwill, Emegha, Quenda, Gusto, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao.
Referee: Andrew Madley
VAR: Lewis Smith
Preamble
Since returning to the Premier League in 2022, Nottingham Forest have yet to win this particular fixture. They’ve lost it three out of four times, though, the most recent defeat a 3-0 shellacking last October that got Ange Postecoglou the sack 15 minutes after the final whistle. Nobody’s expecting Oliver Glasner to get the old heave-ho should Forest extend their miserable record tonight, but with the Tricky Trees currently above the relegation places only thanks to goal difference, the Austrian could do with three precious points and a little time and space.
But it’s his opposite number Xabi Alonso who is under the real pressure tonight. Chelsea are eighth in the table and could go fifth tonight, a scenario that usually doesn’t merit the sounding of the crisis klaxon. But they were hammered 4-1 at home by big rivals Leeds last weekend, their second Premier League defeat in a row and their third in four matches. The defence is in tatters, the midfield falls apart when Moisés Caicedo isn’t there, the style of play is yet to be determined, and the boss used to play for Liverpool. Another defeat would set the cat, if not among the pigeons, then a couple of paces behind them, quietly waiting for the most effective moment to pounce.
The good news for Chelsea: that aforementioned record at the City Ground. The good news for Forest: they’ve already beaten Manchester City at home, and won at Stamford Bridge back in May. So good luck conf

Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.
France's Melenchon visits Berlin to plug book, meet Left Party
French hard-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon visited Berlin on Friday, and said he sees "a need for a thorough overhaul of the Franco-German relationship."
Melenchon, who is hoping the radical economic platform he's championed for decades in France might finally resonate with voters in the vacuum left by Emmanuel Macron as he hits term limit in April's presidential elections, said he opposed the German government's spending and defense policies.
"I am hostile to the liberal [economic] policy of German governments that dominates the European Union," the 75-year-old said.
Melenchon advocates drastically increasing public spending in France, already the much more debt-laden of the EU's top two economies, and canceling French debt held by the European Central Bank in order to do so — a step that critics argue would risk damaging both France and Europe's economies more generally.
The 75-year-old said he also rejected Chancellor Friedrich Merz's plan to increase German defense spending.
"We have the duty to ask: to make war against whom," Melenchon said, warning that a stronger Germany could make nuclear-armed France and the rest of Europe a "target" for other countries.
"They need to tone it down, because this one-upmanship leads nowhere," he said.
Melenchon has enshrined leaving NATO and nationalizing defense companies in his party's election platform, prompting allegations of him cosying up to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
He rejected the notion that he was "Germanophobic," citing his political or musical affection for Karl Marx and Beethoven.
He touted his party's ties with Germany's Left Party (die Linke) and met with party chair Ines Schwerdtner in the capital on Friday while plugging the German translation of his book.
The Left, too, has criticized Germany's defense spending plans. It's increasingly vague on the question of NATO, no longer explicitly calling for an immediate exit as it once did, but still advocating "replacing" NATO with some other kind of collective European security architecture.
IN PICTURES — Opening night festivities at Nuremberg's Christmas market
Germans in favor of continued European military support for Ukraine — survey
European military backing for Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion continues to enjoy widespread support in Germany, according to the results of a new survey published on Friday.
The representative "Politbarometer" poll published by public broadcaster ZDF found that 37% of Germans consider the current level of European support for Ukraine to be just right, while another 31% think it should be increased. Fewer than 30% were in favor of a reduction in military support.
The survey also found that almost two thirds of Germans (64%) think Russia poses a large (39%) or very large (25%) threat to Germany, while the rest consider the threat posed by Moscow to be not so big (23%) or non-existent (11%).
When broken down politically, the survey found that supporters of almost all parties consider the danger posed by Russia to be big or very big. Only far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voters bucked the trend with 75% believing that Moscow poses either no threat at all or only a minor one.
The ZDF survey results differ slightly from those published by the Körber foundation on Tuesday, which suggested for the first time that German military backing for Ukraine no longer enjoyed majority support among the population.
The ZDF survey, however, asked respondents about "European" support for Ukraine rather than about Germany specifically.
Former German spy chief loses detention appeal
A former German spy chief who is accused of acquiring confidential information supplied to him by a former bureau chief has lost his appeal against pre-trial detention.
August Hanning, the former head of Germany's federal intelligence service (Bundesnachrichtendienst or BND) from 1998-2005, was arrested in October on suspicion of purchased highly sensitive documents from his former colleague and using them as part of intelligence analyses in his role as a private consultant.
Hanning is suspected of having prepared one such analysis for Azerbaijan's domestic intelligence service, although it's unclear whether or not classified information ever actually reached Baku.
At the start of November, Hanning's lawyer appealed against what he called a "disproportionate" pre-trial detention, telling Der Spiegel news magazine that his client had not given away any state secrets nor had the intention of doing so. He also told the dpa news agency that Hanning, 80, did not pose a flight risk.
However, the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof or BGH) has rejected the appeal.
German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans
German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63."
At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.
In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.

items.text:
New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
- Published
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.
Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.
The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.
Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".
This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.
Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.
Satellites give a clearer picture
In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.
But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.
Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.
"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".
The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.
The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.
If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.
Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.
Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.
Sinking caused by local activities
The man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.
One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.
The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.
In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.
Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops.
"Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.
The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.
The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.
Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

Kyle Shanahan's San Francisco 49ers are the best team in football. Is this finally the season they win a Lombardi Trophy? Their next test is against the champions.
Most offenses in the NFL look and function the way they do because of the Shanahan. His fingerprints, and still that of his father, have long been ingrained in trends, wrinkles and schematic interpretations dominant across the league as fans know it.
He tops the tree that has shaped modern football. And he is beating them all at his own game. He has done so for some time, minus the shiny reward at the end.
In that sense he sits alongside Josh Allen, even Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson, in likely believing he would have a ring were it not for Patrick Mahomes, Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs' Super Bowl dynasty, which twice have taken down Shanahan's 49ers in the season finale.
But the Niners look good for another Championship run. And few deserve it quite like Shanahan.

- Eagles sink Cowboys with historic Thanksgiving NFL comeback

It would be a staggering case study were he not to win a Super Bowl at some stage in San Francisco, bearing in mind not only the number of close calls for a team he has led to four NFC Championship Games - two of which he won - in nine seasons, but also the genius football brain that has governed sidelines and film rooms across the nation.
His 49ers sit 9-1 in pole position for the No 1 seed in the NFC heading into Sunday night's matchup with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. They do so having just dismantled the Minnesota Vikings and their league-leading scoring defense 35-10 in Mexico City; only twice this season had teams put up more than 20 points against Brian Flores' defense. Shanahan torched them with ease.
It was a message to teams across the league, many of which had been foiled by Flores, his blitz bombardments and camouflaged coverages. It, too, was further evidence of an expertly drilled operation that stormed past the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia in kickoff week before making Mexico home in famously tricky high-altitude conditions. Should they win a Super Bowl, the NFL's 'are they really world champions?' debate loses some substance; the Niners have gone global.
Shanahan's offense entered Week 12 ranked second in yards per game, sixth in passing, fourth in rushing and No 1 in scoring while topping all teams in EPA/play and success rate as the most prolific attack in football.
At the heart of it is Brock Purdy, who Shanahan both identified and cultivated from Mr Irrelevant to undeniable MVP candidate. Non-Purdy believers had deemed him the product of the Shanahan system; to admit that could be partly true would be a deserved nod to what San Francisco's head coach does as one of football's masterminds. Nonetheless, Purdy has proven he is more than a mere puppet surrounded by stars.
Purdy is 206 of 290 passing (71 per cent) for 2,624 yards and 23 touchdowns to just five interceptions with a league-high passer rating of 118.2. It should be noted he has missed practice this week due to an ankle issue. So stay tuned.
He is wildly accurate, underrated as a creator outside of the pocket, clinical in decision-making, aggressive enough to attack downfield and an outstanding diagnostician. The win over Minnesota in Mexico was the newest addition to his MVP resume, behind which Shanahan has been phenomenal.
Purdy was 16 of 18 for 195 yards and two touchdowns when facing the blitz, while finishing eight of nine for 100 yards when pressured during blitzes, according to NextGen Stats. It would contribute to an offensive display that saw the Vikings managed an EPA per dropback of 0.613; no other team had surpassed 0.037 EPA per dropback against Minnesota entering Week 11, per Pro Football Focus. His head coach is putting him in positions for success, and Purdy is executing.
"He's the best player in the game right now. He's super dialled in, the way he prepares, the way he competes," said wide receiver Mike Evans. "He's tough. I always thought he's been underrated, his precision. Super smart player."
Purdy may not win MVP with Joe Burrow around. And Shanahan probably will not win Coach of the Year. That doesn't mean he isn't the best coach in the NFL.
In many ways he and Purdy are a match made in heaven, perfectly suited to one another. They are also thriving together in the face of seemingly never-ending injury obstacles.
They lead an old guard of veteran weapons, who sense another championship campaign.
George Kittle has been Purdy's most targeted pass catcher with 47 catches for a team-high 591 and seven touchdowns, while Christian McCaffrey has over 1,000 yards from scrimmage with a second-most 14 total touchdowns. Mike Evans is the big-bodied one-on-one target Purdy and Shanahan have been missing, but has missed time through injury, and Deebo Samuel is channelling his wide back days again, but has missed time through injury.
"You have to at some point put Purdy in the MVP conversation with what he's been able to do for this 49ers team," said Sky Sports NFL's Phoebe Schecter.
"I think it's hard not to look at what happened in Mexico City and not feel like this team is unstoppable, even with a litany of injuries that are going on."

items.text:
Tyson Fury's manager reveals Anthony Joshua called him to check December 11 fight was going ahead after schizophrenia claim
Spencer Brown has reaffirmed Tyson Fury's fight against Anthony Joshua will go ahead on December 11; Paris Fury retracted comments made in a new Netflix documentary that her husband had Schizophrenia; the British Boxing Board of Control cleared Fury to fight on Friday
Friday 27 November 2026 19:23, UK
Tyson Fury's manager Spencer Brown revealed Anthony Joshua called him to check if their fight was still going ahead, after claims the 'Gypsy King' had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.
Paris Fury made the claims during a new Netflix documentary about her husband's life, but later retracted her comments, clarifying: "[Fury] doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."
While some had raised questions over whether the 38-year-old would be able to fight, the British Boxing Board of Control [BBBoC], on Friday, announced it had cleared Fury, adding he had passed pre-fight tests.
- Bakole welcomes 'danger' in Wilder fight on Fury vs Joshua bill
- Dubois vs Parker announced for WBO heavyweight title clash
- Fury vs Joshua latest news
Speaking to Dev Sahni, Brown flatly dismissed claims that their December 11 fight was in jeopardy.
"Even Anthony Joshua rang me and said: 'Is this fight going on, because I've heard rumours that his licence…" Brown said.
"I said: 'One-million per cent [the fight is on], just turn up and be there. The fight's happening; it's unbelievable'."
Fury posted on Instagram on Friday night to explain how delighted he was about the launch of his new documentary TYSON FURY, urging fans to watch the film, before adding: "The journey continues, next stop December 11."
Netflix says it has worked to "update" the footage in light of Paris' clarification on Thursday.
The documentary explores Fury's experiences with depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder after they became acute following his 2015 world championship victory over Wladimir Klitschko.
Brown said the 38-year-old was more focused on his training rather than speculation about the fight.
"To him, it's a load of old rubbish from 10 years ago," Brown said.
"Obviously, it's reared its head. People have decided to make an issue of it, when there is no issue. And people panicked a little bit. So, there is no issue. The fight goes on."
Brown added: "It's been noted and everybody knows that Tyson has suffered from a mental illness. And we all know that. It's out everywhere.
"That was a long time ago, he's very happy, and I've never seen him in a better headspace, to be quite honest."
Fury's manager also revealed the lengths his team are going to to help the Wythenshawe-born fighter prepare for the bout.
"I speak to him nearly every day," he said.
"Some mundane things about, we have to make sure that he's travelled right and he's in his hotel and that wherever he's staying, every minute thing has to be done right, down to the windows being blacked out.
"Because he's on a different sleep pattern because they're fighting late at night.
"We have to make sure that he's got solitude, and he's happy, and he's smiling every day. His food is there, transport is there.
"His security are there. Everything has to be done to a specification."
Brown also issued a warning to Joshua ahead of the fight.
"If you're listening, Anthony Joshua, the fight's on," Brown said. "Get ready. Make sure that chin of yours is solid. Because it's going to need to be."

items.text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.
Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war
I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.
We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.
Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.
Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. items.summary:
Qatar GP: Kimi Antonelli completes Friday practice double as Mercedes dominate despite red-flag interruptions
Kimi Antonelli and George Russell delivered a one-two for Mercedes in Practice Two despite having their soft-tyre runs interrupted by red flags; watch final practice at 2.30pm ahead of Quali
items.text:
Qatar GP: Kimi Antonelli completes Friday practice double as Mercedes dominate despite red-flag interruptions
Kimi Antonelli and George Russell delivered a one-two for Mercedes in Practice Two despite having their soft-tyre runs interrupted by red flags; watch final practice at 2.30pm ahead of Qualifying at 6pm on Saturday live on Sky Sports F1
Friday 27 November 2026 18:33, UK
Kimi Antonelli topped his team-mate George Russell in both of Friday's practice sessions at the Qatar Grand Prix as Mercedes produced a dominant showing.
Antonelli's time of 1:23.077s saw him finish just over a tenth of a second clear of Russell in Practice Two, with McLaren's Lando Norris almost half a second down on the leading effort in third.
The Silver Arrows were clear of their rivals despite both having what should have been their fastest laps of the session - on fresh soft tyres - blown by two separate red flags, with the leading times set on their earlier medium-tyre runs.
- Qatar GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports

- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Russell had been more than three tenths up on Antonelli's session-topping time after two sectors when a first red flag was thrown to allow the clearance of debris left on track after Ferrari's Charles Leclerc had spun.
Following that stoppage, Antonelli had gone a tenth up on his leading time in the first sector when Pierre Gasly spun at high speed at Turn 14, leaving his Alpine beached in the gravel.
An extra 13 minutes was added to the end of the session to recover some of the lost time, but after the second red flag the field focused on race simulations, during which Mercedes were also extremely impressive.
Friday's action was something of a throwback to Mercedes' dominance during the early stages of the season, which saw Antonelli and the team build leads that have helped them already secure the drivers' and constructors' championships.
The hugely impressive display came as something of a surprise given Mercedes have won just one of the last six races, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen winning four of those.
Verstappen was just behind Norris and the other McLaren of Oscar Piastri in fifth, and marginally ahead of his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, with all four around half a second down on Antonelli despite having done their fastest laps on the theoretically quicker soft tyre.
A disappointing day for Ferrari ended with Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton seventh and eighth, respectively, with both failing to get soft-tyre flying laps completed.
Leclerc missed 20 minutes of track action after damaging his car's floor, while Hamilton was interrupted by the red flags and errors of his own.
Hamilton suffered an apparent engine failure in the closing moments of the session, but the issue is not expected to leave him requiring new parts and he should therefore avoid a grid penalty for Sunday's race.
Hamilton was also involved in a strange incident with Verstappen that saw the pair almost make contact on the main straight, but the stewards decided a full investigation wasn't necessary after noting the Brit for driving erratically.
High levels of tyre degradation throughout both of Friday's session offered something of an explanation for Pirelli's decision to introduce a 27-lap tyre limit for Sunday's race, which will create a two-stop race.
It is the third time a tyre limit has been implemented for the race at the Lusail International Circuit after punctures at the inaugural 2021 event and safety concerns being raised during the 2023 weekend.

items.text:
Repository navigation
Description
Three skills in this plugin (listed in Anthropic's claude-plugins-official marketplace) raised the same concern for me:
- skills/quickstart/SKILL.md lines 48 to 56 POST the user's one-sentence project idea to basic-anteater-667.convex.site, marked in a comment as telemetry. The user is not told the idea leaves the machine.
- skills/add/SKILL.md lines 62 and 64 pipe a script from the same host straight into bash.
- skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md lines 74 to 80 split downloading and running the bootstrap into two Bash calls, and give the reason: "A single command that both downloads remote code and executes it is the shape harness safety classifiers block."
I read this as a team trying to make onboarding reliable, not as anything malicious. But the last item tells the agent to change the shape of a command so that the user's safety tooling does not catch it, which removes the check the user or their administrator chose to have. Together with an unpinned script from a generated-name host, a user has no way to review what runs.
convex-backend-skill/skills/quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 48 to 56 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/add/SKILL.md
Lines 58 to 65 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 74 to 80 in 6ca54f6
(All three are still on main as of 26 October; in labs-quickstart the passage is now lines 73 to 80.)
Suggestions: tell the user before the idea is sent, and make it optional; ship the bootstrap and add scripts in the plugin (or pin them by hash) instead of fetching them at run time; and drop the instruction about the classifier, letting the download-and-run step be approved or refused as it is.
I maintain a catalog of agent skills and of the tools for vetting them; it lists these findings at https://thirtysix.github.io/awesome-agent-skills/#skills?q=convex and I will add your response.
Activity
- And I who was just looking at giving Convex my money.
But now will probably instead look more closely at the alternatives I was already looking at.

items.text:
Emery praises Garnacho attitude after Villa selection snub
- Published
Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has praised Alejandro Garnacho's "fantastic attitude" -but suggested other players rank ahead of him after the Argentine was left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.
The 22-year-old winger joined Aston Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer, but he has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season.
Garnacho was left at home for the 2-0 loss by Galatasaray, with Emery bringing 11 substitutes - including two goalkeepers - rather than the maximum 12.
"When he is not involved in the squad it is because I have to choose with other players as well," said the Villa boss on Friday.
"He has my respect first as a person and second as a player, but he is not involved for this reason.
"But football can change. We are playing matches so I will need players."
- Not even making a 12-man bench - what next for Garnacho? 
  - Published1 day ago
Garnacho has played in just four of Villa's 11 Premier League matches this season and has yet to start across all competitions, coming off the bench for all seven of his appearances.
His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.
"Alejandro Garnacho is training very well. His attitude is fantastic, very good attitude," Emery added.
"He was struggling at the beginning of the season because he was not fit. Now he is fit and he's training at a good level."
Sources have acknowledged Garnacho was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.
He initially trained on his own, while his problems were not helped by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season.
"Of course now he, and other players as well, are performing well, they are working well, they understood how we are building the squad," Emery said.
"It's not how it was two months ago when he wasn't fit enough to be playing with the consistency we needed.
"So keep going, keep moving forward as a club, as a team, he himself as a player and we will see it."
Garnacho's move to Villa will become permanent for £43m at the end of the season should certain criteria be met, but there are concerns his time at the club could become similar to that of Harvey Elliot, who played just nine times last season after arriving on loan from Liverpool.
Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the Major League Soccer - meaning Garnacho could feature for another team, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.
However, Emery said he was not thinking about the upcoming January transfer window as he added: "It is November, of course there is a transfer window in January, but we are not thinking about the transfer window in January. Me especially."
Analysis: Situation could leave players & clubs thinking twice on loan moves
Does this damage Villa after Elliott lost a year of his career last season?
There was already talk in the game of how players could be fearful it could happen to them - and that caution may increase with Garnacho's situation.
Having happened twice in two seasons it would also leave clubs with second thoughts too given the players are their assets.
Garnacho has managed just 95 minutes across all competitions, having joined Villa to revive a faltering career after an inconsistent first season at Chelsea.
Head of football operations Damian Vidagany was unrepentant when asked about the winger at a fans' forum on Thursday, with Emery's trusted lieutenant fiercely backing the manager's judgement call.
Villa, though, arguably need a player like Garnacho - who can produce moments of magic like his stunning goal for Manchester United against Everton in 2023 - having failed to score in four of their last six winless games.
Emery wanted a pacy winger in the summer and the Argentine had been on their wanted list all year.
They need some need some creativity, so with Emery, at least publicly, refusing to rule out a January departure there could still be a slim chance of redemption.

Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths

items.text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
- assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
- engaging in organised criminal activity
- radicalisation
- facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
- being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
- Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders 
  - Published19 October
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Additional reporting by Thomas Mukhwana

items.title: Football Daily | Watford, the Pozzos and the hottest managerial seat in the game
items.summary:
HELLO, GOODBYE
A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic
items.text:
HELLO, GOODBYE
A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic, Xisco Muñoz, Claudio Ranieri, Roy Hodgson, Rob Edwards, Slaven Bilic, Chris Wilder, Valérien Ismael, Tom Cleverley, Paulo Pezzolano and Edward Still in being sacked by the Pozzo family since 2012. There was no denial on Sunday, when the axe inevitably fell on the head coach following a 4-0 shellacking at Sheffield United and the Italian left after only 18 games in charge. While his reign is unlikely to live long in the memory of anyone at Vicarage Road, Dionisi can at least boast on his LinkedIn page that in terms of longevity under the Pozzos, he took charge of 18 more matches than Dyche, 17 more than García and 16 more than McKinlay. Indeed, he even outlasted Rob Edwards, who was assured he would be backed “come hell or high water” upon his 2022 appointment, only to be fired from the ejector seat 11 games later.
It’s been quite the white-knuckle ride for Watford since the Pozzos arrived, armed only with a spreadsheet, an army of Udinese cast-offs and knowledge of the loophole that there was no Football League cap on the number of players who could be brought in on loan from clubs outside the UK. And while few fans will be able to recall all 25 of the coaches who have been hired and fired by the Pozzos, they do have fond memories to take to the grave. There was that end-to-end Troy Deeney play-off semi-final goal against Leicester. There were five uninterrupted seasons in the Premier League. There was that time they ended Liverpool’s 44-match unbeaten Premier League run despite being stuck in the relegation zone. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling to watch their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?
Of course it hasn’t all been rosy in the Pozzo garden. The eight-day managerial reign of McKinlay was a source of much mirth for fans of rival clubs. A double relegation from the Premier League – the first amid allegations of a dressing-room bust-up linked to an illegal lockdown party – wasn’t great either. Playing I’m Still Standing by Elton John, the club’s honorary life president, over the Vicarage Road PA system to mark their descent into the Championship heaped further embarrassment upon the club. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling home after watching their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?
While it would be foolish to predict what will happen next at a club that currently sit two places above the Championship relegation zone, the one stonewall certainty is that the name “Edward Iordanescu” will be the next to be copied and pasted into the over-worked club template announcing a managerial departure. The Romanian was formally introduced this morning and with this being his 14th job in the past 16 years, he can arguably lay claim to being the most ‘Watford’ manager of the Pozzo era. “For me, I want a team that plays very good, organised football with the spirit and attitude, and the strong mentality,” he blathered, as local reporters dabbed their bingo cards. “And then, yes, regarding the organisation of the team, that takes time.” History suggests getting the time he needs is a pipe dream for Iordanescu, whose first game in charge is away at Championship basement-dwellers Derby County. Should Watford go to Pride Park and lose, he could be out of a job by Saturday night.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Scott Murray from 8pm for red-hot updates on Nottingham Forest 0-0 Chelsea in the Premier League.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“I know people expect me to say: ‘Oh, I regret it.’ No, I don’t regret it. If I regret something, it’s that I would love to kick him in another [place]. The kung fu kick was criticised a lot, especially by journalists. But now it’s a [more positive] symbol. So I change everything” – Eric Cantona is in scintillating form during this chat with Donald McRae.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 
 If you’ve never tried listening to or watching the utter drivel that is ‘The Overlap’, this will mean nothing whatsoever, but if you have, this, by the great Jonathan Liew, is absolutely superb. Satire so biting it even surpasses Luis Suárez at his 2010, 2013 and 2014 peaks” – Noble Francis.
 
 I read your depressing piece about Burnley (yesterday’s Football Daily, full email edition). I am in the unfortunate position of being a season ticket holder at Turf Moor and residing in south-east London. A typical Saturday home game starts for me at 6am, involves two train journeys, the underground and a bus ride (that’s each way) getting home about midnight. Then there is the travel and food costs which are usually in the three figures. Evening games, like Wednesday, involve two days and a friend’s spare room. As a 70-year-old is it too much to expect a similar effort from those overpaid prancing show ponies that think they are too good for Burnley, too good for the Championship – if it’s only just for two hours on match day? There, I’ve said it and I feel much better. That is , of course, until 5pm on Saturday” – Chris Harrison.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Chris Harrison. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

items.text:
Saturday tips: Kap Vert fancied to lift Coral Gold Cup crown at Newbury
Wendigo heads the market for a typically competitive renewal of the Coral Gold Cup at Newbury, with Mr Hope Street, Road To Home and Kap Vert among the challengers; Panic Attack back to defend her crown for in-form Dan Skelton team
Friday 27 November 2026 16:28, UK
With a hugely exciting renewal of the Coral Gold Cup on Saturday, Kate Tracey, Declan Rix and Sam Boswell headed to Newbury for a very special episode of Weekend Winners.
The familiar trio have each had a close look at the famous handicap clash as well as a brilliant supporting card, all live on Sky Sports Racing from 11am.
Jamie Snowden's Wendigo is the pre-race favourite and promises to bring the house down if scoring for the well-supported Racing Club syndicate, while last year's winner Panic Attack returns with 10lb claimer Dominic Lewis on board for the in-form Dan Skelton team.
- Newbury's Coral Gold Cup: Jamie Lynch's horse-by-horse guide
- Three for the Coral Gold Cup! Sean Boyce's Newbury preview
At The Races' Declan Rix…
"My horse is Kap Vert. He's only a six-year-old but for a novice to go and win the Scottish National I thought was a big effort.
"All he's done is progress and improve. This horse's big asset is his jumping and he's got a prominent style of racing, which I like for the track.
"If the rain does come, we know he's going to handle that and it puts more emphasis on his stamina.
"It's a big ride for Sean Houlihan and if he can bounce him out early and get into a rhythm, his jumping will keep him in it."
Host Kate Tracey…
"I don't want too much rain to come down for my pick: Miami Magic.
"He had the perfect prep for this, in my opinion, in a Pertemps Qualifier here on November 5.
"It didn't exactly go to plan early on in his chasing career but I think he's got his act together now.
"I'm hoping it will be fair ground for him to bounce off."
BetVictor's Sam Boswell…
"It's unoriginal, but I'm with Wendigo. It's competitive from a betting angle but I think it looks a little bit shy of real top-class future chasers.
"This is the one horse who could maybe be that and he's 40/1 for the Grand National.
"The trip is the one thing people might throw at him because he's an old-fashioned chaser who needs a bit of getting after but once he does, he'll stay on really nicely.
"For me, he's the standout. He's a really strong and obvious contender. For Jamie Snowden and the Lambourn trainers, this is their Cheltenham Gold Cup. This is a special race and I think it will go to a local trainer."

items.text:
Spurs' Savio to miss festive fixtures after injury setback
- Published
Tottenham winger Savio will miss the club's Christmas fixtures with injury and could be out for up to 80 days, manager Roberto de Zerbi has confirmed.
Savio joined Spurs from Manchester City for £75m this summer, but has played in just five of their 11 Premier League matches this season.
The 22-year-old came on as a substitute in the 64th minute of Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich on Saturday, but was forced off with two minutes remaining with a hamstring injury.
It was the attacker's first game back in six weeks after returning from a muscle problem which led to him missing the four previous league matches.
Asked if Savio, previously known as Savinho, would miss the Christmas schedule, De Zerbi said: "Yes, I think so unfortunately.
"It is a tough situation to accept. He is a good guy. He is suffering for this new injury but it is part of football."
"If you see the other European clubs, all of them, they are suffering many, many injuries."
Savio is still searching for his first league goal or assist for Tottenham, although he did score and assist a goal on his debut in August in a 5-1 win over Charlton in the Carabao Cup.
"Now, he needs time and hard work with the medical staff," De Zerbi added.
"Then in 50, 60 or 80 days - I don't know when he comes back - he'll be crucial for us for the last step of the season."
Tottenham are 10th in the league and have won four of their past five matches after a poor start to the season.
They travel to 18th-placed Sunderland on Sunday (14:05 GMT).
